## modern-en · argives · 1:2

There is another point too that strongly confirms my view of the weakness of earlier times. Before the Trojan War there is no sign of any common action across Hellas, nor indeed of the universal use of the name. On the contrary, before the time of Hellen, son of Deucalion, no such name existed at all; the country went by the names of its various tribes, and chiefly by that of the Pelasgians. Only when Hellen and his sons grew strong in Phthiotis, and were brought in as allies by other cities, did those cities one by one acquire the name Hellenes through the connection — though even then a long time passed before that name attached itself to all of them. The best proof comes from Homer. Born long after the Trojan War, he nowhere calls them all Hellenes, nor in fact any of them, except for the followers of Achilles from Phthiotis, who were the original Hellenes. In his poems they are called Danaans, Argives, and Achaeans. He does not even use the word barbarian, probably because the Hellenes had not yet been set apart from the rest of the world by a single distinctive name. So it appears that the various Hellenic communities — both those who first acquired the name, city by city, as they came to understand each other, and those who later adopted it as the name of the whole people — were before the Trojan War prevented by their lack of strength and their isolation from one another from achieving any collective action.

Sparta’s enemy, whom the Athenians allied with the moment they were sent home from Ithome, and a thousand of whom marched with them to Tanagra. Themistocles in exile lived among them and kept secret hoards there.

So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships, set up a democracy there, took fifty boys and as many men from the Samians as hostages, lodged them on Lemnos, left a garrison on the island, and went home. But some of the Samians had not stayed on the island; they had fled to the mainland. Coming to an arrangement with the most powerful of those left in the city, and forming an alliance with Pissuthnes, son of Hystaspes, then satrap of Sardis, they got together a force of seven hundred mercenaries and crossed over to Samos under cover of night. Their first move was to rise against the commons, most of whom they secured; their next was to steal back their hostages from Lemnos. Siege-works were now raised and manned by the Athenians on the isthmus side of the wall. On the Pallene side none were raised. They did not feel strong enough at once to keep a garrison on the isthmus and cross over to Pallene to raise works there; they feared that the Potidæans and their allies might take advantage of their division to attack them. Meanwhile the Athenians at home, learning that there were no works on the Pallene side, some time later sent out sixteen hundred heavy infantry of their own citizens under the command of Phormio, son of Asopius. On reaching Pallene he fixed his headquarters at Aphytis and led his army against Potidæa by short marches, ravaging the country as he advanced. Since no one ventured to meet him in the field, he raised works against the wall on the Pallene side. So at last Potidæa was strongly invested on both sides, and from the sea by the ships cooperating in the blockade. Aristeus, seeing the investment complete and having no hope of saving the place except in the event of some movement from the Peloponnese, or some other improbable contingency, advised that all but five hundred men should watch for a wind and sail out of the place, so that provisions might last longer. He was willing to remain himself among those who stayed. Unable to persuade them, and wishing to take the next best course and have things outside in the best possible state, he eluded the Athenian guardships and sailed out. Remaining with the Chalcidians, he carried on the war: in particular he laid an ambush near the city of the Sermylians and cut off many of them; he also communicated with the Peloponnese and tried to contrive some method of bringing help. The allies of the two belligerents were these. On the Lacedaemonian side: all the Peloponnesians within the Isthmus except the Argives and Achaeans, who were neutral; Pellene was the only Achaean city that joined in the war from the start, though the others followed her lead later. Outside the Peloponnese: the Megarians, Locrians, Boeotians, Phocians, Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians. Of these, ships were supplied by the Corinthians, Megarians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Eleans, Ambraciots, and Leucadians; cavalry by the Boeotians, Phocians, and Locrians. The other states sent infantry. That was the Lacedaemonian confederacy. The Athenian confederacy consisted of the Chians, Lesbians, Plataeans, the Messenians at Naupactus, most of the Acarnanians, the Corcyraeans, the Zacynthians, and various tributary cities in the following regions: Caria on the coast with her Dorian neighbours, Ionia, the Hellespont, the Thracian towns, the islands lying between the Peloponnese and Crete to the east, and all the Cyclades except Melos and Thera. Of these, ships were supplied by Chios, Lesbos, and Corcyra; the rest provided infantry and money. Such were the allies of either side, and such their resources for the war.

## modern-en · molossians · 5:18

To return to the Medism of Pausanias. Material was found in the course of the inquiry that implicated Themistocles. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the Athenians, demanding that he be punished as Pausanias had been. The Athenians agreed. As it happened, however, he had been ostracised, and, while living at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of the Peloponnese. So the Athenians sent agents along with the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join the pursuit, with instructions to take him wherever they found him. But Themistocles got wind of their intentions and fled from the Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations to him. The Corcyraeans claimed they could not risk sheltering him at the cost of offending Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the continent opposite. Pursued by officers who hung on every report of his movements, at a loss where to turn, he was forced to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on friendly terms. Admetus happened not to be at home, but his wife, to whom he made himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the hearth. Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was and begged him not to take revenge on a Themistocles in exile for any opposition his requests might have met from Themistocles at Athens. He was now far too low for revenge; retaliation was honourable only between equals. Besides, his opposition to the king had affected only the success of a request, not the safety of his person; if the king were to hand him over to the pursuers he had mentioned, and to the fate they intended for him, he would simply be consigning him to certain death.

Admetus’s people, with whom Themistocles took sanctuary.

The Lacedaemonians had once raised some Helot suppliants from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away, and killed them; for which they believe the great earthquake at Sparta was retribution. The Athenians also ordered them to drive out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House, the history of which is as follows. After Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont (this was his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted, he was not sent out again in any official capacity. He took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility, without Lacedaemonian authority, and arrived as a private person in the Hellespont. He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, but really to pursue his intrigues with the King, which he had begun before his recall, ambitious to rule over Hellas. The circumstance that first allowed him to put the King in his debt and to begin the whole design was this. Some of the King’s connections and kinsmen had been captured at Byzantium when the city was taken from the Medes, when Pausanias was first there after the return from Cyprus. He sent these prisoners off to the King without the knowledge of the rest of the allies, with the cover story that they had escaped. He arranged this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had put in charge of Byzantium and the prisoners. He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of which—as was later discovered—were as follows: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta, eager to do you a favour, sends you these prisoners of war. I propose also, with your approval, to marry your daughter and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you. I believe I am able to do this, with your cooperation. So if any of this pleases you, send a trusty man to the sea through whom we may carry on our future correspondence.”

Whose old war with Chalcis was the nearest thing to a coalition in Hellas before the Median War; and Gongylus was one of them.

What enabled Agamemnon to raise that force was, in my opinion, more his superiority in strength than the oaths of Tyndareus, which bound the suitors to follow him. The account given by those Peloponnesians who have inherited the most credible tradition runs as follows. Pelops first arrived from Asia among a needy population, bringing vast wealth, and acquired such power that, foreigner though he was, the country was named after him. Fortune saw fit to increase that power further in the hands of his descendants. Eurystheus had been killed in Attica by the Heraclids. Atreus was his mother's brother. To this kinsman — who had left his father after the death of Chrysippus — Eurystheus, when he set out on his expedition, had entrusted Mycenæ and the government. As time passed and Eurystheus did not return, Atreus, at the wish of the Mycenaeans, who feared the Heraclids — and since his power seemed considerable, and he had taken care to court the favour of the people — took up the sceptre of Mycenæ and the rest of Eurystheus's dominions. And so the power of the descendants of Pelops came to surpass that of the descendants of Perseus. To all this Agamemnon succeeded. He also had a fleet far stronger than any of his contemporaries, so that in my opinion it was fear quite as much as goodwill that drew the joint expedition together. The strength of his navy is shown by the fact that his own contingent was the largest, and that the Arcadians' ships were supplied by him — at least if we accept Homer on this. ## modern-en · epidaurians · 4:11

Meanwhile the Athenians, making a landing from their fleet at Haliae, were engaged by a force of Corinthians and Epidaurians, and the Corinthians won. Afterwards the Athenians fought the Peloponnesian fleet off Cecruphalia, and the Athenians won. Then war broke out between Aegina and Athens. There was a great sea battle off Aegina between Athenians and Aeginetans, each side helped by their allies; the Athenians won, taking seventy of the enemy’s ships. They landed and began a siege of the country under the command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus. At this the Peloponnesians, wanting to help the Aeginetans, threw three hundred heavy infantry — who had previously been serving with the Corinthians and Epidaurians — into Aegina. Meanwhile the Corinthians and their allies seized the heights of Geraneia and marched down into the Megarid, in the belief that with so large an Athenian force absent in Aegina and Egypt, Athens would be unable to help the Megarians without lifting the siege of Aegina. But the Athenians, instead of moving the army at Aegina, raised a force from the old men and the boys who had been left in the city, and marched into the Megarid under the command of Myronides. After a drawn battle with the Corinthians, the two sides parted, each thinking they had won. The Athenians had rather the better of it, and after the Corinthians left they set up a trophy. Stung by taunts from the elders in their city, the Corinthians made their preparations and about twelve days later came back and set up their own trophy as victors. Sallying out from Megara, the Athenians cut off the party that was setting up the trophy, then engaged and defeated the rest. As the beaten army retreated, a sizeable detachment, hard pressed by the pursuers and missing the road, blundered into a piece of private land surrounded by a deep trench, with no way out. Knowing the place, the Athenians sealed off the front with heavy infantry, posted light troops in a ring around it, and stoned to death every man inside. This was a heavy blow to Corinth. The allies of the two belligerents were these. On the Lacedaemonian side: all the Peloponnesians within the Isthmus except the Argives and Achaeans, who were neutral; Pellene was the only Achaean city that joined in the war from the start, though the others followed her lead later. Outside the Peloponnese: the Megarians, Locrians, Boeotians, Phocians, Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians. Of these, ships were supplied by the Corinthians, Megarians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Eleans, Ambraciots, and Leucadians; cavalry by the Boeotians, Phocians, and Locrians. The other states sent infantry. That was the Lacedaemonian confederacy. The Athenian confederacy consisted of the Chians, Lesbians, Plataeans, the Messenians at Naupactus, most of the Acarnanians, the Corcyraeans, the Zacynthians, and various tributary cities in the following regions: Caria on the coast with her Dorian neighbours, Ionia, the Hellespont, the Thracian towns, the islands lying between the Peloponnese and Crete to the east, and all the Cyclades except Melos and Thera. Of these, ships were supplied by Chios, Lesbos, and Corcyra; the rest provided infantry and money. Such were the allies of either side, and such their resources for the war.

Who with the Lesbians alone were never deprived of their ships and made to pay money instead, and who sent twenty-five ships to the siege of Samos.

## modern-en · phaeacians · 2:1

When the Epidamnians found that no help could be expected from Corcyra, they did not know what to do next. So they sent to Delphi and asked the god whether they should hand over their city to the Corinthians and try to obtain some assistance from their founders. The god answered that they should hand over the city and place themselves under Corinthian protection. The Epidamnians went to Corinth and surrendered the colony in obedience to the oracle. They pointed out that their founder had come from Corinth, repeated the god’s answer, and begged the Corinthians not to let them perish but to assist them. The Corinthians agreed. They believed the colony belonged as much to themselves as to the Corcyraeans, and they felt a kind of duty to take its protection in hand. Besides, they hated the Corcyraeans for the contempt they showed the mother country. Other colonies honoured Corinth at public assemblies in the usual ways—precedence at sacrifices, for instance—but Corcyra treated her with contempt. And Corcyra was wealthy enough to stand comparison with the richest communities in Hellas, militarily strong, and at times openly proud of her naval reputation, which dated back to her old inhabitants, the Phaeacians. This was one reason the Corcyraeans took such care of their fleet, which became very efficient: they began the war with a force of one hundred and twenty galleys.

Corcyra’s old inhabitants, from whom the Corcyraeans date the naval reputation they were at times openly proud of.

## modern-en · argilians · 5:15

At the time the Lacedaemonians had erased the couplet at once and inscribed instead the names of the cities that had aided in the overthrow of the barbarian and dedicated the offering. Pausanias was considered to have been guilty of a grave offence here—one which, interpreted in the light of the attitude he had since taken, gained a new significance and seemed perfectly in keeping with his current schemes. They were also informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots; and so it was, for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in revolt and help him carry out his plans to the end. Even now, mistrusting the evidence even of the Helots themselves, the ephors would not consent to take any decisive step against him, in line with their regular custom toward fellow Spartans—to be slow to take any irrevocable decision in the case of a Spartan citizen without indisputable proof. At last, it is said, the man who was to carry the latest letter to Artabazus for the King, an Argilian and once Pausanias’s favourite and most trusted servant, turned informer. Alarmed by the thought that none of the previous messengers had ever returned, he had counterfeited the seal so that, if he were mistaken in his suspicions, or if Pausanias asked to make some change, he would not be found out. He undid the letter and found the postscript he had suspected—an order to put him to death.

One of them was Pausanias’s favourite and most trusted servant, and the courier who counterfeited the seal, found the postscript ordering his own death, and turned informer.

## modern-en · chrysis-argos · 6:1

The thirty years’ truce that was made after the conquest of Euboea lasted fourteen years. In the fifteenth, in the forty-eighth year of the priestess-ship of Chrysis at Argos, in the ephorate of Aenesias at Sparta, in the last month but two of the archonship of Pythodorus at Athens, and six months after the battle of Potidæa, just at the beginning of spring, a Theban force a little over three hundred strong, under the command of their Boeotarchs, Pythangelus, son of Phyleides, and Diemporus, son of Onetorides, made an armed entry into Plataea — a town in Boeotia allied with Athens — about the first watch of the night. The gates were opened to them by a Plataean named Naucleides, who, with his party, had invited them in. They intended to put to death the citizens of the opposite faction, hand the city over to Thebes, and so secure power for themselves. The arrangements had been made through Eurymachus, son of Leontiades, a man of great influence at Thebes. For Plataea had always been at odds with Thebes; and Thebes, foreseeing that war was at hand, wanted to surprise her old enemy in peacetime, before hostilities had actually broken out. This was how they got in so easily, unobserved: no guard had been posted. Once the soldiers had grounded arms in the marketplace, those who had let them in wanted them to set to work at once and go to the houses of their enemies. The Thebans refused, and decided instead to make a conciliatory proclamation and, if possible, to come to a friendly understanding with the citizens. Their herald accordingly invited any who wished to take their old place in the confederacy of their countrymen to ground arms with them; they thought the city would readily come over to them this way.

The priestess of Hera at Argos, in the forty-eighth year of whose office the war began. Thucydides dates the outbreak by her, by the ephor at Sparta and by the archon at Athens, because there was no common calendar. Not Eumachus’s father.

Once the soldiers had grounded arms in the marketplace, those who had let them in wanted them to set to work at once and go to the houses of their enemies. The Thebans refused, and decided instead to make a conciliatory proclamation and, if possible, to come to a friendly understanding with the citizens. Their herald accordingly invited any who wished to take their old place in the confederacy of their countrymen to ground arms with them; they thought the city would readily come over to them this way.

The thirty years’ truce that was made after the conquest of Euboea lasted fourteen years. ## modern-en · cecrops · 6:15

From very early times this had been more the case with the Athenians than with others. Under Cecrops and the first kings, down to the reign of Theseus, Attica had always consisted of a number of independent townships, each with its own town hall and magistrates. Except in times of danger the king at Athens was not consulted; in normal seasons they ran their government and settled their affairs without his involvement; sometimes they even went to war against him, as in the case of the Eleusinians under Eumolpus against Erechtheus. With Theseus, however, they had a king of equal intelligence and power. One of the chief features of his reorganization of the country was to abolish the council-chambers and magistrates of the smaller cities and merge them into the single council-chamber and town hall of the present capital. Individuals could still enjoy their private property as before, but they were now compelled to have only one political centre — Athens — which thus counted all the inhabitants of Attica among her citizens. So when Theseus died he left a great state behind him. From him, indeed, dates the Synoecia, or Feast of Union, which is paid for by the state and which the Athenians still hold in honour of the goddess. Before this, the city consisted of the present citadel and the district just below it, facing more towards the south. This is shown by the fact that the temples of the other deities, besides that of Athene, are in the citadel; and even those that are outside it are mostly in this part of the city — like the temple of Olympian Zeus, of Pythian Apollo, of Earth, and of Dionysus in the Marshes (the same in whose honour the older Dionysia are still celebrated to this day in the month of Anthesterion, not only by the Athenians but by their Ionian descendants too). There are other ancient temples in this quarter as well. The fountain too, which since the alteration made by the tyrants has been called Enneacrounos, or Nine Pipes, but which when the spring was open went by the name of Callirhoe, or Fairwater, was in those days, because it was so close, used for the most important purposes. Indeed, the old custom of using its water before marriage and for other sacred purposes is still kept up. And from their old residence in that quarter, the citadel is still called by the Athenians “the city.”

Under whom, and the first kings after him, Attica was a country of independent townships.

## modern-en · polymedes · 6:24

He, meanwhile, seeing anger and folly in the ascendant for the moment, and confident in the wisdom of his refusal to fight, would not call either an assembly or a meeting of the people, fearing the disastrous results of a debate driven by passion rather than prudence. He devoted himself to the defence of the city and kept it as quiet as possible, while constantly sending out cavalry to prevent raids on the lands near the city by stray parties of the enemy. There was a minor affair at Phrygia between a squadron of Athenian horse with the Thessalians and the Boeotian cavalry, in which the Athenians had rather the better of it until the heavy infantry came up to support the Boeotians, when the Thessalians and Athenians were routed and lost a few men, whose bodies, however, were recovered the same day without a truce. The next day the Peloponnesians set up a trophy. An ancient alliance brought the Thessalians to Athens’ aid; the contingents that came were from Larisa, Pharsalus, Cranon, Pyrasus, Gyrton, and Pherae. The Larisaean commanders were Polymedes and Aristonus, two party leaders in Larisa; the Pharsalian general was Menon; each of the other cities had its own commander as well.

## modern-en · brasidas · 6:27

Meanwhile the Athenians in the hundred ships round the Peloponnese, reinforced by a Corcyraean squadron of fifty ships and others from the allies in those parts, cruised the coasts and ravaged the country. Among other places, they landed in Laconia and made an assault on Methone, where there was no garrison and the wall was weak. As it happened, Brasidas, son of Tellis, a Spartan, was in command of a guard for the defence of the district. On hearing of the attack, he hurried with a hundred heavy infantry to relieve the besieged, and dashing through the Athenian army, which was scattered over the country with its attention on the wall, he threw himself into Methone. He lost a few men in forcing his way in, but he saved the place and won the gratitude of Sparta by his exploit, becoming the first officer to gain such recognition in the war. The Athenians at once weighed anchor and continued their cruise. Touching at Pheia in Elis, they ravaged the country for two days and defeated a picked force of three hundred men who had come from the vale of Elis and the immediate neighbourhood to the rescue. But a stiff squall came down on them, and not wanting to face it in a place with no harbour, most of them went on board their ships, doubled Point Ichthys, and sailed into the port of Pheia. In the meantime the Messenians, and some others who could not get on board, marched over by land and took Pheia. The fleet later sailed round, picked them up, and put to sea; Pheia was abandoned, since the main army of the Eleans had now come up. The Athenians continued their cruise and ravaged other places along the coast.

Tellis’s son. In command of a guard in Laconia when the Athenians assaulted Methone, he ran a hundred heavy infantry straight through an army scattered over the country, lost a few men getting in, and saved the place — the first officer in the war to be publicly commended at Sparta. He was sent out afterwards as one of the three commissioners to stiffen Cnemus’s fleet, and was in the party that talked itself out of the raid on Piraeus. The older translation misprints him Bradidas once.

## modern-en · nymphodorus · 6:31

During the same summer Nymphodorus, son of Pythes, an Abderite whose sister was married to Sitalces, was made the Athenians’ proxenus and summoned to Athens. They had hitherto considered him their enemy; but he had great influence with Sitalces, and they wanted this prince as their ally. Sitalces was the son of Teres and king of the Thracians. Teres, the father of Sitalces, had been the first to establish the great Odrysian kingdom on a scale quite unknown to the rest of Thrace, since a large part of the Thracians were independent. This Teres is in no way related to the Tereus who married Pandion’s daughter Procne from Athens; indeed they did not even belong to the same part of Thrace. Tereus lived in Daulis, in what is now called Phocis, but which at that time was inhabited by Thracians. It was in this land that the women perpetrated the outrage on Itys, and many of the poets, when they mention the nightingale, call it the Daulian bird. Besides, Pandion in arranging an alliance for his daughter would consider the advantages of mutual help, and would naturally prefer a match at this moderate distance to the journey of many days that separates Athens from the Odrysians. Again the names are different; and this Teres was king of the Odrysians — the first, by the way, to attain any power. Sitalces, his son, was now sought as an ally by the Athenians, who wanted his help in the reduction of the Thracian towns and of Perdiccas. Coming to Athens, Nymphodorus concluded the alliance with Sitalces, made his son Sadocus an Athenian citizen, and promised to bring the Thracian war to a close by persuading Sitalces to send the Athenians a force of Thracian horse and targeteers. He also reconciled the Athenians with Perdiccas, and got them to restore Therme to him, on which Perdiccas at once joined the Athenians and Phormio in an expedition against the Chalcidians. So Sitalces, son of Teres, king of the Thracians, and Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, became allies of Athens.

Pythes’s son, an Abderite whose sister was married to Sitalces. Athens had counted him an enemy and now made him her proxenus and sent for him: he brought in the Thracian alliance, got Sitalces’s son Sadocus made an Athenian citizen, and reconciled Athens with Perdiccas.

Sitalces, his son, was now sought as an ally by the Athenians, who wanted his help in the reduction of the Thracian towns and of Perdiccas. Coming to Athens, Nymphodorus concluded the alliance with Sitalces, made his son Sadocus an Athenian citizen, and promised to bring the Thracian war to a close by persuading Sitalces to send the Athenians a force of Thracian horse and targeteers. He also reconciled the Athenians with Perdiccas, and got them to restore Therme to him, on which Perdiccas at once joined the Athenians and Phormio in an expedition against the Chalcidians. So Sitalces, son of Teres, king of the Thracians, and Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, became allies of Athens.

Teres’s son and king of the Thracians, whose alliance Athens bought with a citizenship for his son and the return of Therme to Perdiccas. He came down into Macedonia with a hundred and fifty thousand men, a third of them horse, and frightened every people between Thermopylae and the Danube — and then, with no provisions and bad weather, took his nephew’s advice and went home after thirty days, having achieved none of it.

## modern-en · evarchus · 6:32

Meanwhile the Athenians in the hundred ships were still cruising round the Peloponnese. After taking Sollium, a town belonging to Corinth, and presenting the city and its territory to the Acarnanians of Palaira, they stormed Astacus, expelled its tyrant Evarchus, and brought the place into their confederacy. Next they sailed to the island of Cephallenia and brought it over without using force. Cephallenia lies off Acarnania and Leucas and consists of four states — Pale, Crane, Same, and Pronae. Not long afterwards the fleet returned to Athens. Towards the autumn of this year the Athenians invaded the Megarid with their full levy, including the resident aliens, under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus. The Athenians in the hundred ships round the Peloponnese, on their way home, had just reached Aegina when, hearing that the citizens at home were in full force at Megara, they sailed over and joined them. This was without doubt the largest army of Athenians ever assembled, the state being still in the flower of her strength and not yet visited by the plague. A full ten thousand heavy infantry were in the field, all Athenian citizens, besides the three thousand before Potidæa. The resident aliens who joined the incursion were at least three thousand strong, and there was a great mass of light troops besides. They ravaged most of the territory and then withdrew. Other incursions into the Megarid were made by the Athenians annually during the war, sometimes with cavalry alone, sometimes with all their forces. This continued until the capture of Nisaea. Atalanta also, the desert island off the Opuntian coast, was towards the end of this summer turned into a fortified post by the Athenians, to keep privateers from sailing out of Opus and the rest of Locris and plundering Euboea. Such were the events of this summer after the return of the Peloponnesians from Attica.

Tyrant of Astacus, expelled by the hundred ships and put back by forty Corinthian ones the following winter, partly with mercenaries he hired himself.

## modern-en · euphamidas · 6:33

In the following winter the Acarnanian Evarchus, wanting to return to Astacus, persuaded the Corinthians to sail over with forty ships and fifteen hundred heavy infantry and reinstate him; he himself also hired some mercenaries. In command of the force were Euphamidas, son of Aristonymus, Timoxenus, son of Timocrates, and Eumachus, son of Chrysis. They sailed over and reinstated him; and after failing in an attempt on some places along the Acarnanian coast that they wanted to gain, they began their voyage home. Coasting along, they touched at Cephallenia and made a descent on Cranian territory. Losing some men through the treachery of the Cranians, who fell on them suddenly after agreeing to terms, they put to sea in some haste and went home.

Aristonymus’s son, first-named of the three commanders of the forty Corinthian ships that restored Evarchus.

## modern-en · acharnians · 6:22

The reason Archidamus stayed in battle order at Acharnae during this incursion, instead of going down into the plain, is said to have been this. He hoped the Athenians might be tempted, by the size of their younger generation and the unprecedented strength of their armed services, to come out to battle and try to stop the destruction of their lands. Accordingly, since they had not met him at Eleusis or on the Thriasian plain, he tested whether they could be provoked to a sortie by the spectacle of a camp at Acharnae. He thought the place itself was a good site for a camp; and he reckoned that such an important segment of the state as the three thousand heavy infantry of the Acharnians would refuse to put up with the ruin of their property and would force a battle on the rest of the citizens. On the other hand, if the Athenians did not take the field during this incursion, he could safely ravage the plain in future invasions and push his advance right up to the walls of Athens. After the Acharnians had lost their own property, they would be less willing to risk themselves for that of their neighbours; and so there would be division in the Athenian counsels. Those were Archidamus’ motives for staying at Acharnae.

Of the largest of the Athenian demes, three thousand heavy infantry of them — which is why Archidamus camped on their land and waited, reckoning they would force a battle on the rest of the city; and they were the loudest in pressing for the sortie.

## modern-en · pellenians · 6:8

The allies of the two belligerents were these. On the Lacedaemonian side: all the Peloponnesians within the Isthmus except the Argives and Achaeans, who were neutral; Pellene was the only Achaean city that joined in the war from the start, though the others followed her lead later. Outside the Peloponnese: the Megarians, Locrians, Boeotians, Phocians, Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians. Of these, ships were supplied by the Corinthians, Megarians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Eleans, Ambraciots, and Leucadians; cavalry by the Boeotians, Phocians, and Locrians. The other states sent infantry. That was the Lacedaemonian confederacy. The Athenian confederacy consisted of the Chians, Lesbians, Plataeans, the Messenians at Naupactus, most of the Acarnanians, the Corcyraeans, the Zacynthians, and various tributary cities in the following regions: Caria on the coast with her Dorian neighbours, Ionia, the Hellespont, the Thracian towns, the islands lying between the Peloponnese and Crete to the east, and all the Cyclades except Melos and Thera. Of these, ships were supplied by Chios, Lesbos, and Corcyra; the rest provided infantry and money. Such were the allies of either side, and such their resources for the war.

Of the one Achaean city that joined the war from the start, the rest following her lead later.

## modern-en · nicias-father-of-hagnon · 7:13

The same summer Hagnon, son of Nicias, and Cleopompus, son of Clinias, the colleagues of Pericles, took the force he had recently used and went off on an expedition against the Chalcidians around Thrace and Potidæa, which was still under siege. As soon as they arrived, they brought up their engines against Potidæa and tried every means of taking it, but did not succeed in capturing the city or in doing anything else worthy of their preparations. The plague attacked them here too, and committed such havoc as to cripple them completely; even the previously healthy soldiers from the earlier expedition caught the infection from Hagnon’s troops, while Phormio and the sixteen hundred men under his command escaped only by being no longer in the area of the Chalcidians. The end of it was that Hagnon returned with his ships to Athens, having lost one thousand and fifty out of four thousand heavy infantry in about forty days; though the soldiers stationed there before stayed in the country and carried on the siege of Potidæa.

Hagnon’s father. Neither the Cretan of Gortys nor the Athenian general of the later books.

## modern-en · aneristus · 7:22

At the end of the same summer Aristeus the Corinthian, Aneristus, Nicolaus, and Stratodemus — envoys from Lacedaemon — Timagoras, a Tegean, and a private individual named Pollis from Argos, on their way to Asia to persuade the King to supply funds and join the war, came to Sitalces, son of Teres, in Thrace. Their idea was to induce him, if possible, to abandon the Athenian alliance and march on Potidæa, then under siege by an Athenian force, and also to be conveyed by his help across the Hellespont to Pharnabazus, who would send them up country to the King. But there happened to be with Sitalces some Athenian ambassadors — Learchus, son of Callimachus, and Ameiniades, son of Philemon — who persuaded Sitalces’ son Sadocus, the new Athenian citizen, to put the men into their hands and so prevent their crossing over to the King and helping to harm the country he had chosen. Sadocus accordingly had them seized as they were travelling through Thrace to the ship in which they were to cross the Hellespont. The seizure was carried out by a party he had sent on with Learchus and Ameiniades, with orders to deliver the men to the Athenian ambassadors, who brought them to Athens. On their arrival, the Athenians, afraid that Aristeus, who had notably been the prime mover in earlier affairs at Potidæa and in their Thracian possessions, might survive to do them still more harm if he escaped, killed them all the same day, without granting them a trial or hearing the defence they wished to offer, and threw their bodies into a pit. They thought themselves justified in using in retaliation the same kind of warfare that the Lacedaemonians had begun, when they had killed and thrown into pits all the Athenian and allied traders they caught on board the merchantmen round the Peloponnese. Indeed, at the start of the war, the Lacedaemonians butchered as enemies all whom they took at sea, whether allies of Athens or neutrals.

One of the envoys Lacedaemon sent to the King for money, seized in Thrace by Sadocus and killed at Athens the same day without a trial.

## modern-en · amphilochus · 7:23

About the same time, towards the close of the summer, the Ambraciot forces, with a number of barbarians they had raised, marched against Amphilochian Argos and the rest of that country. The origin of their enmity against the Argives was this. This Argos and the rest of Amphilochia were colonized by Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus. Dissatisfied with the state of affairs at home on his return after the Trojan War, he built this city in the Ambracian Gulf and named it Argos after his own country. This was the largest town in Amphilochia, and its inhabitants the most powerful. Generations later, under the pressure of misfortune, they called in the Ambraciots, their neighbours on the Amphilochian border, to join their colony. It was through this union with the Ambraciots that they learned their present Hellenic speech; the rest of the Amphilochians are barbarians. After a time the Ambraciots expelled the Argives and held the city themselves. At this the Amphilochians threw in their lot with the Acarnanians, and together they called in the Athenians, who sent them Phormio as general with thirty ships; on whose arrival they took Argos by storm and made slaves of the Ambraciots. The Amphilochians and Acarnanians then inhabited the town in common. After this began the alliance between Athenians and Acarnanians. The enmity of the Ambraciots toward the Argives thus dates from the enslavement of their citizens; and afterwards, during the war, they collected this force from among themselves, the Chaonians, and other neighbouring barbarians. Arriving before Argos, they became masters of the country; but failing in their attacks on the town, they returned home and dispersed among their various peoples.

Amphiaraus’s son, who came home from Troy dissatisfied with the state of affairs, built a city in the Ambracian gulf and named it Argos after his own country.

## modern-en · melesander · 7:24

Such were the events of the summer. The following winter the Athenians sent twenty ships round the Peloponnese, under the command of Phormio, who stationed himself at Naupactus and kept watch on anyone sailing in or out of Corinth and the Crissaean Gulf. Six others went to Caria and Lycia under Melesander to collect tribute in those parts, and also to prevent the Peloponnesian privateers from setting up a base in those waters and harassing the passage of merchantmen from Phaselis, Phoenicia, and the adjoining mainland. Melesander, however, going up country into Lycia with a force of Athenians from the ships and the allies, was defeated and killed in battle, with the loss of a number of his troops.

Who took six ships to Caria and Lycia to collect tribute and keep the Peloponnesian privateers from setting up there — and was defeated and killed going up country into Lycia.

## modern-en · xenophon-euripides · 7:25

The same winter the Potidæans at last found themselves no longer able to hold out against their besiegers. The Peloponnesian invasions of Attica had not had the desired effect of making the Athenians raise the siege. Provisions were exhausted, and distress for food in Potidæa had gone so far that, among many other horrors, instances had even occurred of people eating one another. In this extremity they at last made proposals to capitulate to the Athenian generals in command against them — Xenophon, son of Euripides, Hestiodorus, son of Aristocleides, and Phanomachus, son of Callimachus. The generals accepted their proposals, seeing the suffering of the army in such an exposed position; besides, the state had already spent two thousand talents on the siege. The terms of capitulation were as follows: free passage out for themselves, their children, wives, and auxiliaries, with one garment apiece, two for the women, and a fixed sum of money for their journey. Under this treaty they went out to Chalcidice and other places, as their means allowed. The Athenians, however, blamed the generals for granting terms without instructions from home, holding that the place would have had to surrender at discretion. They afterwards sent their own settlers to Potidæa and colonized it. Such were the events of the winter; and so ended the second year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.

Euripides’s son, first-named of the three Athenian generals who took Potidaea’s capitulation, and afterwards the commander beaten and killed at Spartolus.

## modern-en · cnemus · 7:21

During the same summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies made an expedition with a hundred ships against Zacynthus, an island off the coast of Elis, peopled by a colony of Achaeans from the Peloponnese and in alliance with Athens. There were a thousand Lacedaemonian heavy infantry on board, and Cnemus, a Spartan, as admiral. They made a landing from their ships and ravaged most of the country; but as the inhabitants would not submit, they sailed home.

The Spartan high admiral: he ravaged Zacynthus and got nowhere, slipped past Phormio into the gulf with a thousand heavy infantry and a barbarian army, lost the Chaonians to an ambush at Stratus, and had three commissioners sent out in anger to stiffen him after his fleet was beaten in the Crissaean gulf.

## modern-en · photys · 8:9

That same summer, not long after this, the Ambraciots and Chaonians, wishing to reduce the whole of Acarnania and detach it from Athens, persuaded the Lacedaemonians to fit out a fleet from their confederacy and send a thousand heavy infantry to Acarnania. Their argument was that, if a combined movement were made by land and sea, the coastal Acarnanians would be unable to march; that the conquest of Zacynthus and Cephallenia would easily follow on the possession of Acarnania, so that the cruise round the Peloponnese would no longer be so convenient for the Athenians; and besides this, there was a hope of taking Naupactus. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent off at once a few vessels with Cnemus, who was still high admiral, and the heavy infantry on board, and sent round orders for the rest of the fleet to be readied as quickly as possible and to sail to Leucas. The Corinthians were the most active in the business, since the Ambraciots were a colony of theirs. While the ships from Corinth, Sicyon, and the surrounding region were getting ready, and those from Leucas, Anactorium, and Ambracia, which had arrived earlier, were waiting for them at Leucas, Cnemus and his thousand heavy infantry had run into the gulf, slipping past Phormio, the commander of the Athenian squadron stationed off Naupactus, and at once began to prepare for the land expedition. The Hellenic troops with him consisted of the Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians, and the thousand Peloponnesians he had brought; the barbarian troops, of a thousand Chaonians, who, belonging to a nation that has no king, were led by Photys and Nicanor, the two members of the royal family entrusted with the chieftainship for that year. With the Chaonians came also some Thesprotians, who like them had no king, some Molossians and Atintanians led by Sabylinthus, the guardian of King Tharyps, who was still a minor, and some Paravaeans under their king Oroedus, accompanied by a thousand Orestians, subjects of King Antiochus, placed by him under the command of Oroedus. There were also a thousand Macedonians sent by Perdiccas without the knowledge of the Athenians, but they arrived too late. With this force Cnemus set out, without waiting for the fleet from Corinth. Passing through the territory of Amphilochian Argos, sacking the open village of Limnaea, they advanced to Stratus, the Acarnanian capital. Once that was taken, they were convinced, the rest of the country would soon follow.

One of the two members of the Chaonian royal family entrusted with the chieftainship for the year; the Chaonians have no king.

## modern-en · machaon · 8:12

Meanwhile the fleet from Corinth and the rest of the confederates in the Crissaean Gulf, which was supposed to cooperate with Cnemus and prevent the coastal Acarnanians from joining their countrymen in the interior, was prevented from doing so by being forced, about the time of the battle at Stratus, to fight Phormio and the twenty Athenian vessels stationed at Naupactus. As they coasted along out of the gulf, they were watched by Phormio, who wanted to attack in open sea. The Corinthians and their allies had set out for Acarnania with no intention of fighting at sea, and with vessels more like transports for carrying soldiers; besides which, they never imagined that the twenty Athenian ships would venture to engage their forty-seven. However, while they were coasting along their own shore, there were the Athenians sailing in line with them; and when they tried to cross over from Patrae in Achaea to the mainland on the other side, on their way to Acarnania, they saw them again coming out from Chalcis and the river Evenus to meet them. They slipped from their moorings during the night, but were spotted, and at last were forced to fight in mid-passage. Each state that contributed to the armament had its own general; the Corinthian commanders were Machaon, Isocrates, and Agatharchidas. The Peloponnesians arranged their vessels in as large a circle as possible without leaving an opening, prows outward and sterns inward; and they placed inside the circle all the small craft accompanying them, along with their five best sailers, who were to issue out at a moment's notice and reinforce any point threatened by the enemy.

One of the three Corinthian commanders of the forty-seven ships Phormio broke in the mouth of the Crissaean gulf.

## modern-en · timocrates-sparta · 8:14

The Lacedaemonians now sent three commissioners — Timocrates, Brasidas, and Lycophron — to Cnemus's fleet, with orders to prepare to engage again with better fortune, and not to be driven from the sea by a few vessels. They could not at all account for the defeat, especially as it was their first attempt at sea, and they imagined that it was not that their navy was so inferior, but that there had been misconduct somewhere — not taking into account the long experience of the Athenians compared with the little practice they had had themselves. The commissioners were therefore sent in anger. As soon as they arrived they set to work with Cnemus to order ships from the various states and to put the ones they already had into fighting order. Meanwhile Phormio sent word to Athens of their preparations and of his own victory, asking that as many ships as possible be sent to him quickly, since he was in daily expectation of a battle. Twenty were accordingly sent, but their commander was instructed to go first to Crete. For Nicias, a Cretan of Gortys who was proxenus of the Athenians, had persuaded them to sail against Cydonia, promising to bring about the reduction of that hostile town. His real wish was to oblige the Polichnitans, neighbours of the Cydonians. He accordingly went with the ships to Crete, and, accompanied by the Polichnitans, laid waste the lands of the Cydonians; and, with adverse winds and bad weather, wasted a good deal of time there.

One of the three Lacedaemonian commissioners sent out in anger after the first defeat. He was aboard the Leucadian that an Athenian ship sank off a merchantman at Naupactus, killed himself when she went down, and was washed up in the harbour. Not Timoxenus’s father.

## modern-en · amyntas · 8:24

About the same time, at the beginning of this winter, Sitalces, son of Teres, the Odrysian king of Thrace, made an expedition against Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of Macedonia, and against the Chalcidians in the neighbourhood of Thrace. His object was to enforce one promise and fulfil another. On the one hand, Perdiccas, when hard pressed at the start of the war, had made him a promise on condition that Sitalces would reconcile the Athenians to him and not try to restore his brother and enemy, the pretender Philip; but Perdiccas had not offered to fulfil his side of the deal. On the other hand, Sitalces himself, on entering into alliance with the Athenians, had agreed to put an end to the Chalcidian war in Thrace. These were the two aims of his invasion. He brought with him Amyntas, son of Philip, whom he intended for the throne of Macedonia; some Athenian envoys then at his court on this business; and Hagnon as general — for the Athenians were to join him against the Chalcidians with a fleet and as many soldiers as they could muster.

Philip’s son, whom Sitalces brought with him and intended for the throne of Macedonia; Idomene, Gortynia and Atalanta came over out of attachment to him.

## modern-en · seuthes · 8:26

The empire of the Odrysians extended along the seaboard from Abdera to the mouth of the Danube on the Euxine. Sailing along this coast by the shortest route takes a merchantman four days and four nights with a wind astern the whole way; by land, an active man, going by the shortest road, can get from Abdera to the Danube in eleven days. Such was the length of its coastline. Inland, from Byzantium to the Laeaeans and the Strymon — the farthest extent of the empire into the interior — is a journey of thirteen days for an active man. The tribute from all the barbarian districts and Hellenic cities, taking what came in under Seuthes, the successor of Sitalces, who raised it to its greatest height, amounted to about four hundred talents in gold and silver. There were also presents in gold and silver to no smaller a sum, besides cloth, plain and embroidered, and other articles, made not only for the king but also for the Odrysian lords and nobles. The custom established here was the opposite of that in the Persian kingdom: it was a custom of taking rather than giving, more disgrace being attached to refusing to give when asked than to asking and being refused. Although this prevailed elsewhere in Thrace, it was practised most extensively among the powerful Odrysians, since nothing could be done without a present. It was thus a very powerful kingdom, surpassing in revenue and general prosperity all the kingdoms of Europe between the Ionian Gulf and the Euxine, and in numbers and military resources coming clearly next to the Scythians, with whom indeed no people in Europe can be compared — there is not even any nation in Asia that singly is a match for them when they are united, though of course they are not on a level with other races in general intelligence and the arts of civilized life.

Spardacus’s son, Sitalces’s nephew and highest officer, and afterwards his successor, who raised the Odrysian tribute to four hundred talents. Perdiccas secretly bought him with the promise of his sister, and he advised the retreat; Perdiccas gave him Stratonice as promised.

## modern-en · spardacus · 8:31

Meanwhile Sitalces opened negotiations with Perdiccas on the objects of his expedition. Finding that the Athenians, not believing he would come, did not appear with their fleet (though they sent presents and envoys), he detached a large part of his army against the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, shut them inside their walls, and laid waste their country. While he remained in these parts, the peoples farther south — the Thessalians, Magnetes, the other tribes subject to the Thessalians, and the Hellenes as far as Thermopylae — all feared that the army might advance against them, and made their preparations accordingly. These fears were shared by the Thracians beyond the Strymon to the north, who inhabited the plains — the Panaeans, Odomanti, Droi, and Dersaeans, all of whom are independent. It was even a matter of conversation among the Hellenes who were enemies of Athens whether he might not be invited by his ally to advance against them too. Meanwhile he held Chalcidice, Bottice, and Macedonia, and was ravaging them all; but finding that he was succeeding in none of the objects of his invasion, and that his army was without provisions and suffering from the severity of the weather, he listened to the advice of Seuthes, son of Spardacus, his nephew and highest officer, and decided to retreat without delay. Seuthes had been secretly won over by Perdiccas, who promised him his sister in marriage with a rich dowry. Following this advice, and after a stay of thirty days in all, eight of which were spent in Chalcidice, he withdrew home as quickly as he could; and Perdiccas afterwards gave his sister Stratonice to Seuthes as he had promised. Such was the history of the expedition of Sitalces.

Seuthes’s father. The history spells him Spardacus in Book 2 and Sparadocus in Book 4.

These Macedonians, unable to take the field against so numerous an invader, shut themselves up in such strongholds and forts as the country possessed. There were not many of these — most of those now found in the country having been built later by Archelaus, son of Perdiccas, on his accession, who also cut straight roads and otherwise put the kingdom on a better footing as regards horses, heavy infantry, and other military equipment than all the eight kings before him had done. Advancing from Doberus, the Thracian host first invaded what had once been Philip's government, and took Idomene by assault, and Gortynia, Atalanta, and some other places by negotiation — these last coming over out of attachment to Philip's son, Amyntas, then with Sitalces. He laid siege to Europus, but failed to take it; he then advanced into the rest of Macedonia, to the left of Pella and Cyrrhus, but did not press beyond this into Bottiaea and Pieria, staying instead to lay waste Mygdonia, Crestonia, and Anthemus.

Perdiccas’s son, who on his accession built most of the strongholds the country has, cut straight roads, and did more for the kingdom’s horses and heavy infantry than the eight kings before him together.

## modern-en · cynes · 8:32

In the course of this winter, after the dispersion of the Peloponnesian fleet, the Athenians in Naupactus, under Phormio, coasted along to Astacus and disembarked, and marched into the interior of Acarnania with four hundred Athenian heavy infantry and four hundred Messenians. After expelling some suspected persons from Stratus, Coronta, and other places, and restoring Cynes, son of Theolytus, to Coronta, they returned to their ships, deciding it was impossible in the winter season to march against Oeniadae, a place that, unlike the rest of Acarnania, had always been hostile to them. For the river Achelous flows from Mount Pindus through Dolopia and the country of the Agraeans and Amphilochians and the plain of Acarnania, past the town of Stratus in its upper course, and forms lakes where it falls into the sea around Oeniadae, making the area impracticable for an army in winter because of the water. Opposite Oeniadae lie most of the islands called the Echinades, so close to the mouths of the Achelous that that powerful stream is constantly piling up deposits against them, and has already joined some of the islands to the mainland, and seems likely before long to do the same with the rest. The current is strong, deep, and muddy, and the islands lie so thick together that they trap the alluvial deposit and prevent it from dispersing — they lie not in one line but irregularly, leaving no direct channel for the water into the open sea. The islands in question are uninhabited and not of any great size. There is also a story that Alcmaeon, son of Amphiaraus, during his wanderings after the murder of his mother, was told by Apollo to settle on this spot, through an oracle which suggested that he would have no release from his terrors until he found a country to live in that had not been seen by the sun, nor existed as land, at the time he killed his mother — for all other ground was polluted to him. Perplexed at this, the story goes on, he at last noticed this deposit of the Achelous, and judged that a place sufficient to support life on might have been thrown up during the long interval that had passed since his mother's death and the beginning of his wanderings. So he settled in the district around Oeniadae, founded a dominion, and gave the country its name from his son Acarnan. Such is the story we have received concerning Alcmaeon.

Theolytus’s son, whom Phormio restored to Coronta.

## modern-en · odrysians · 6:31

During the same summer Nymphodorus, son of Pythes, an Abderite whose sister was married to Sitalces, was made the Athenians’ proxenus and summoned to Athens. They had hitherto considered him their enemy; but he had great influence with Sitalces, and they wanted this prince as their ally. Sitalces was the son of Teres and king of the Thracians. Teres, the father of Sitalces, had been the first to establish the great Odrysian kingdom on a scale quite unknown to the rest of Thrace, since a large part of the Thracians were independent. This Teres is in no way related to the Tereus who married Pandion’s daughter Procne from Athens; indeed they did not even belong to the same part of Thrace. Tereus lived in Daulis, in what is now called Phocis, but which at that time was inhabited by Thracians. It was in this land that the women perpetrated the outrage on Itys, and many of the poets, when they mention the nightingale, call it the Daulian bird. Besides, Pandion in arranging an alliance for his daughter would consider the advantages of mutual help, and would naturally prefer a match at this moderate distance to the journey of many days that separates Athens from the Odrysians. Again the names are different; and this Teres was king of the Odrysians — the first, by the way, to attain any power. Sitalces, his son, was now sought as an ally by the Athenians, who wanted his help in the reduction of the Thracian towns and of Perdiccas. Coming to Athens, Nymphodorus concluded the alliance with Sitalces, made his son Sadocus an Athenian citizen, and promised to bring the Thracian war to a close by persuading Sitalces to send the Athenians a force of Thracian horse and targeteers. He also reconciled the Athenians with Perdiccas, and got them to restore Therme to him, on which Perdiccas at once joined the Athenians and Phormio in an expedition against the Chalcidians. So Sitalces, son of Teres, king of the Thracians, and Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, became allies of Athens.

Teres’s kingdom and Sitalces’s, whose empire ran from Abdera to the Danube and inland thirteen days’ journey, and whose custom was the opposite of the Persian one: more disgrace in refusing a present than in asking for one and being refused. Nothing could be done among them without a present.

## modern-en · chaonians · 7:23

About the same time, towards the close of the summer, the Ambraciot forces, with a number of barbarians they had raised, marched against Amphilochian Argos and the rest of that country. The origin of their enmity against the Argives was this. This Argos and the rest of Amphilochia were colonized by Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus. Dissatisfied with the state of affairs at home on his return after the Trojan War, he built this city in the Ambracian Gulf and named it Argos after his own country. This was the largest town in Amphilochia, and its inhabitants the most powerful. Generations later, under the pressure of misfortune, they called in the Ambraciots, their neighbours on the Amphilochian border, to join their colony. It was through this union with the Ambraciots that they learned their present Hellenic speech; the rest of the Amphilochians are barbarians. After a time the Ambraciots expelled the Argives and held the city themselves. At this the Amphilochians threw in their lot with the Acarnanians, and together they called in the Athenians, who sent them Phormio as general with thirty ships; on whose arrival they took Argos by storm and made slaves of the Ambraciots. The Amphilochians and Acarnanians then inhabited the town in common. After this began the alliance between Athenians and Acarnanians. The enmity of the Ambraciots toward the Argives thus dates from the enslavement of their citizens; and afterwards, during the war, they collected this force from among themselves, the Chaonians, and other neighbouring barbarians. Arriving before Argos, they became masters of the country; but failing in their attacks on the town, they returned home and dispersed among their various peoples.

A nation with no king, led by two of the royal family for a year at a time, and with the highest reputation for courage on that part of the mainland. They would not wait to make camp at Stratus, rushed the town for the sole glory of it, and were cut to pieces from the city and the ambushes.

## modern-en · thesprotians · 8:9

That same summer, not long after this, the Ambraciots and Chaonians, wishing to reduce the whole of Acarnania and detach it from Athens, persuaded the Lacedaemonians to fit out a fleet from their confederacy and send a thousand heavy infantry to Acarnania. Their argument was that, if a combined movement were made by land and sea, the coastal Acarnanians would be unable to march; that the conquest of Zacynthus and Cephallenia would easily follow on the possession of Acarnania, so that the cruise round the Peloponnese would no longer be so convenient for the Athenians; and besides this, there was a hope of taking Naupactus. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent off at once a few vessels with Cnemus, who was still high admiral, and the heavy infantry on board, and sent round orders for the rest of the fleet to be readied as quickly as possible and to sail to Leucas. The Corinthians were the most active in the business, since the Ambraciots were a colony of theirs. While the ships from Corinth, Sicyon, and the surrounding region were getting ready, and those from Leucas, Anactorium, and Ambracia, which had arrived earlier, were waiting for them at Leucas, Cnemus and his thousand heavy infantry had run into the gulf, slipping past Phormio, the commander of the Athenian squadron stationed off Naupactus, and at once began to prepare for the land expedition. The Hellenic troops with him consisted of the Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Anactorians, and the thousand Peloponnesians he had brought; the barbarian troops, of a thousand Chaonians, who, belonging to a nation that has no king, were led by Photys and Nicanor, the two members of the royal family entrusted with the chieftainship for that year. With the Chaonians came also some Thesprotians, who like them had no king, some Molossians and Atintanians led by Sabylinthus, the guardian of King Tharyps, who was still a minor, and some Paravaeans under their king Oroedus, accompanied by a thousand Orestians, subjects of King Antiochus, placed by him under the command of Oroedus. There were also a thousand Macedonians sent by Perdiccas without the knowledge of the Athenians, but they arrived too late. With this force Cnemus set out, without waiting for the fleet from Corinth. Passing through the territory of Amphilochian Argos, sacking the open village of Limnaea, they advanced to Stratus, the Acarnanian capital. Once that was taken, they were convinced, the rest of the country would soon follow.

Who came with the Chaonians into Acarnania and, like them, have no king.

## modern-en · stratians · 8:10

The Acarnanians, finding themselves invaded by a large army on land and threatened by a hostile fleet from the sea, made no combined attempt at resistance, but stayed to defend their homes and sent for help to Phormio. He replied that, with a fleet about to sail from Corinth, it was impossible for him to leave Naupactus unprotected. The Peloponnesians and their allies meanwhile advanced on Stratus in three divisions, intending to encamp near it and to attempt the wall by force if they failed to take it by negotiation. The order of march was as follows: the centre was held by the Chaonians and the rest of the barbarians; the Leucadians and Anactorians and their followers held the right; and Cnemus, with the Peloponnesians and Ambraciots, held the left. The divisions were a long way apart, sometimes even out of sight of each other. The Hellenes advanced in good order, keeping a lookout until they encamped in a strong position. But the Chaonians, full of self-confidence, having the highest reputation for courage among the tribes of that part of the mainland, did not wait to occupy their camp; they rushed on with the rest of the barbarians, thinking they could take the town by assault and claim the sole glory of the enterprise. While they were coming on, the Stratians, becoming aware how things stood and thinking that the defeat of this division would seriously dishearten the Hellenes behind it, set ambushes around the town, and as soon as the Chaonians approached, engaged them at close quarters from the city and from the ambushes. A panic seized the Chaonians, great numbers of them were killed, and as soon as they were seen to give way, the rest of the barbarians turned and fled. Because of the distance by which their allies had outpaced them, neither of the Hellenic divisions knew anything of the battle; they imagined the others were simply hurrying to encamp. When, however, the fleeing barbarians broke in upon them, they opened their ranks to receive them, brought their divisions together, and stayed quiet where they were for the day. The Stratians did not offer to engage them, since the rest of the Acarnanians had not yet arrived; instead they contented themselves with slinging at them from a distance, which distressed them greatly, since no one could move without his armour. The Acarnanians seem to excel at this kind of warfare.

Of the Acarnanian capital, who saw how the invading divisions had strung out, set ambushes round the town, broke the Chaonians between the city and the ambushes, and then slung at the Hellenes from a distance — which, Thucydides says, is the kind of warfare the Acarnanians excel at.

## modern-en · getae · 8:25

Beginning with the Odrysians, he first called out the Thracian tribes subject to him between Mount Haemus, Mount Rhodope, the Euxine, and the Hellespont; next the Getae beyond Haemus, and the other hordes settled south of the Danube in the neighbourhood of the Euxine, who, like the Getae, border on the Scythians and are armed the same way, being all mounted archers. Besides these he summoned many of the independent hill Thracian swordsmen, called Dii and mostly inhabiting Mount Rhodope, some of whom came as mercenaries, others as volunteers. He also summoned the Agrianes and Laeaeans and the rest of the Paeonian tribes in his empire, at the edge of which these lay, extending up to the Laeaean Paeonians and the river Strymon, which flows from Mount Scombrus through the country of the Agrianes and Laeaeans. There the empire of Sitalces ends and the territory of the independent Paeonians begins. Bordering on the Triballi, also independent, were the Treres and Tilataeans, who live north of Mount Scombrus and extend westward as far as the river Oskius. This river rises in the same mountains as the Nestus and the Hebrus — a wild and extensive range connected with Rhodope.

Beyond Haemus, who border on the Scythians and are armed like them, all mounted archers; they supplied more of Sitalces’s cavalry than anyone but the Odrysians.

## modern-en · sintians · 8:27

It was the master of this empire who now prepared to take the field. When everything was ready, he set out on his march for Macedonia, first through his own dominions, then over the desolate range of Cercine, which divides the Sintians and Paeonians, crossing by a road he had cut through by felling the timber on a previous campaign against the Paeonians. Passing over these mountains, with the Paeonians on his right and the Sintians and Maedians on the left, he finally arrived at Doberus in Paeonia, losing none of his army on the march, except perhaps to sickness, but receiving some additions, since many of the independent Thracians volunteered to join him in hope of plunder. The whole is said to have come to a grand total of a hundred and fifty thousand. Most of this was infantry, though about a third was cavalry, supplied chiefly by the Odrysians themselves and next by the Getae. The most warlike of the infantry were the independent swordsmen who came down from Rhodope; the rest of the mixed multitude that followed him was formidable mainly in numbers.

Divided from the Paeonians by the desolate range of Cercine, which Sitalces crossed by a road he had cut himself.

## modern-en · lyncestae · 8:28

Assembling at Doberus, they prepared to descend from the heights into Lower Macedonia, where the dominions of Perdiccas lay. The Lyncestae, Elimiots, and other tribes farther inland, though Macedonians by blood, and allies and dependants of their kindred, still have their own separate governments. The country on the seacoast, now called Macedonia, was first acquired by Alexander, the father of Perdiccas, and his ancestors, originally Temenids from Argos. This was achieved by the expulsion of the Pierians from Pieria, who afterwards settled at Phagres and other places under Mount Pangaeus, beyond the Strymon (indeed, the country between Pangaeus and the sea is still called the Pierian Gulf); by the expulsion of the Bottiaeans, now neighbours of the Chalcidians, from Bottia; by the acquisition in Paeonia of a narrow strip along the river Axius extending to Pella and the sea; and by the addition of the district of Mygdonia, between the Axius and the Strymon, after the expulsion of the Edonians. From Eordia they also drove out the Eordians, most of whom perished, though a few still live around Physca; and the Almopians from Almopia. These Macedonians also conquered places belonging to the other tribes, which are still theirs — Anthemus, Crestonia, Bisaltia, and much of Macedonia proper. The whole is now called Macedonia, and at the time of the invasion of Sitalces, Perdiccas, son of Alexander, was the reigning king.

Macedonians by blood and allies and dependants of their kindred, but with their own separate government.

## modern-en · magnetes · 8:31

Meanwhile Sitalces opened negotiations with Perdiccas on the objects of his expedition. Finding that the Athenians, not believing he would come, did not appear with their fleet (though they sent presents and envoys), he detached a large part of his army against the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, shut them inside their walls, and laid waste their country. While he remained in these parts, the peoples farther south — the Thessalians, Magnetes, the other tribes subject to the Thessalians, and the Hellenes as far as Thermopylae — all feared that the army might advance against them, and made their preparations accordingly. These fears were shared by the Thracians beyond the Strymon to the north, who inhabited the plains — the Panaeans, Odomanti, Droi, and Dersaeans, all of whom are independent. It was even a matter of conversation among the Hellenes who were enemies of Athens whether he might not be invited by his ally to advance against them too. Meanwhile he held Chalcidice, Bottice, and Macedonia, and was ravaging them all; but finding that he was succeeding in none of the objects of his invasion, and that his army was without provisions and suffering from the severity of the weather, he listened to the advice of Seuthes, son of Spardacus, his nephew and highest officer, and decided to retreat without delay. Seuthes had been secretly won over by Perdiccas, who promised him his sister in marriage with a rich dowry. Following this advice, and after a stay of thirty days in all, eight of which were spent in Chalcidice, he withdrew home as quickly as he could; and Perdiccas afterwards gave his sister Stratonice to Seuthes as he had promised. Such was the history of the expedition of Sitalces.

Subject to the Thessalians, and among the peoples who made their preparations when they heard how large Sitalces’s army was.

## modern-en · sicilians · 1:13

But as the power of Hellas grew, and the pursuit of wealth became more pressing, the revenues of the states increased, and tyrannies were established almost everywhere on the strength of those revenues — the older form of government having been hereditary monarchy with defined prerogatives. Hellas began to fit out fleets and apply herself more closely to the sea. The Corinthians are said to have been the first to approach the modern style of naval architecture, and Corinth the first place in Hellas where galleys were built. We have Ameinocles, a Corinthian shipwright, building four ships for the Samians. Counting from the end of this present war, it is nearly three hundred years since Ameinocles went to Samos. Likewise, the earliest sea-fight in history was between the Corinthians and Corcyraeans, about two hundred and sixty years ago, dating from the same point. Set on an isthmus, Corinth had from time immemorial been a commercial hub. In the old days nearly all communication between the Hellenes inside and outside the Peloponnese was carried on overland, and Corinthian territory was the highway it travelled. She therefore had great financial resources — as the epithet “wealthy” given to her by the old poets shows — and this enabled her, when sea trade became more common, to acquire her navy and put down piracy. Since she could provide a market for both branches of the trade, she gained for herself all the power that comes from a large revenue. After this, the Ionians built up great naval strength under Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, and his son Cambyses; and during their war with Cyrus, they commanded for a time the Ionian sea. Polycrates also, the tyrant of Samos, had a powerful navy in the reign of Cambyses, with which he reduced many of the islands, including Rhenea, which he consecrated to the Delian Apollo. Around the same time the Phocaeans, while founding Marseilles, defeated the Carthaginians in a sea-fight. These were the most powerful navies. And even these, although so many generations had passed since the Trojan War, seem to have been made up mainly of the old fifty-oars and long-boats, with few galleys among them. It was only shortly before the Persian War, and the death of Darius the successor of Cambyses, that the Sicilian tyrants and the Corcyraeans acquired any large number of galleys. After these, there were no navies of any consequence in Hellas until the expedition of Xerxes. Aegina, Athens, and others may have had a few vessels, but they were mostly fifty-oars. It was right at the end of this period that the war with Aegina and the prospect of the barbarian invasion enabled Themistocles to persuade the Athenians to build the fleet they fought with at Salamis — and even those vessels did not yet have full decks.
