While the Peloponnesians were still gathering at the Isthmus, or marching before they invaded Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten Athenian generals, realized the invasion was about to happen. It occurred to him that Archidamus, who happened to be his personal friend, might possibly bypass his estate without ravaging it. He might do this either as a personal favour or under instructions from Lacedaemon, with the aim of stirring up suspicion against him — much as had been tried before with the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family. Pericles therefore took the precaution of announcing in the Athenian assembly that, although Archidamus was his friend, this friendship would not be allowed to harm the state; and that if the enemy made an exception of his houses and lands and did not pillage them, he was at once handing them over as public property, so that no suspicion would attach to him. He also gave the citizens advice on their present situation in the same vein as before. They were to prepare for the war and to bring in their property from the country. They were not to go out to battle, but to come into the city and guard it, and to have ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay. They were also to keep a tight rein on their allies, since the strength of Athens was drawn from the money those payments brought in; and success in war depends mainly on conduct and capital — there was no reason for despondency. Apart from other sources of revenue, an average income of six hundred talents of silver came in from the tribute of the allies. There were still six thousand talents of coined silver in the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there, from which money had been taken for the porch of the Acropolis, the other public buildings, and Potidæa. This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in public and private offerings, the sacred vessels for the processions and games, the Median spoils, and similar resources, amounting to five hundred talents. To this he added the treasures of the other temples. These were not insignificant and could fairly be used. If they were ever absolutely driven to it, they could even take the gold ornaments off Athene’s own statue; for the figure contained forty talents of pure gold, and it was all removable. This could be used for survival, but every penny had to be paid back. Such was the financial position — and a satisfactory one. Then they had an army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, plus another sixteen thousand in the garrisons and on home duty at Athens. That was the number on guard at first, in the event of an invasion: it consisted of the oldest and youngest levies and the resident aliens with heavy armour. The Phaleric wall ran for four miles before joining the wall around the city; of this last, nearly five miles were guarded, though part was left without a guard — the stretch between the Long Wall and the Phaleric. Then there were the Long Walls to Piraeus, a distance of about four and a half miles, the outer of which was manned. Lastly, the circuit of Piraeus together with Munychia was nearly seven and a half miles; only half of this, however, was guarded. Pericles also pointed out that they had twelve hundred horse, including mounted archers, sixteen hundred foot archers, and three hundred galleys fit for service. Such were the resources of Athens in each department when the Peloponnesian invasion was looming and hostilities were beginning. Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favourable outcome to the war.

On whose statue there were forty talents of pure gold, all of it removable — which Pericles counted among the city’s resources for a last extremity, to be used and paid back. The other deities’ temples are in the citadel with hers.

## modern-en · dionysus · 6:15

From very early times this had been more the case with the Athenians than with others. Under Cecrops and the first kings, down to the reign of Theseus, Attica had always consisted of a number of independent townships, each with its own town hall and magistrates. Except in times of danger the king at Athens was not consulted; in normal seasons they ran their government and settled their affairs without his involvement; sometimes they even went to war against him, as in the case of the Eleusinians under Eumolpus against Erechtheus. With Theseus, however, they had a king of equal intelligence and power. One of the chief features of his reorganization of the country was to abolish the council-chambers and magistrates of the smaller cities and merge them into the single council-chamber and town hall of the present capital. Individuals could still enjoy their private property as before, but they were now compelled to have only one political centre — Athens — which thus counted all the inhabitants of Attica among her citizens. So when Theseus died he left a great state behind him. From him, indeed, dates the Synoecia, or Feast of Union, which is paid for by the state and which the Athenians still hold in honour of the goddess. Before this, the city consisted of the present citadel and the district just below it, facing more towards the south. This is shown by the fact that the temples of the other deities, besides that of Athene, are in the citadel; and even those that are outside it are mostly in this part of the city — like the temple of Olympian Zeus, of Pythian Apollo, of Earth, and of Dionysus in the Marshes (the same in whose honour the older Dionysia are still celebrated to this day in the month of Anthesterion, not only by the Athenians but by their Ionian descendants too). There are other ancient temples in this quarter as well. The fountain too, which since the alteration made by the tyrants has been called Enneacrounos, or Nine Pipes, but which when the spring was open went by the name of Callirhoe, or Fairwater, was in those days, because it was so close, used for the most important purposes. Indeed, the old custom of using its water before marriage and for other sacred purposes is still kept up. And from their old residence in that quarter, the citadel is still called by the Athenians “the city.”

Of the Marshes, in whose honour the older Dionysia are still held in Anthesterion — by the Athenians and by their Ionian descendants.

The Mitylenians, however, were informed of the expedition by a man who crossed from Athens to Euboea, went overland to Geraestus, and from there sailed in a merchantman he found about to put to sea, reaching Mitylene on the third day after leaving Athens. He took the relief fleet to Lesbos so slowly that Mitylene had fallen seven days before he heard of it; refused Teutiaplus’s advice to fall on Paches at night, refused the Ionian exiles’ advice to raise Ionia, butchered his prisoners at Myonnesus until Samian envoys told him this was no way to free Hellas, and fled home across the open sea. At Corcyra he would not attack the town even when Brasidas urged it. He was afterwards one of the three founders of Heraclea in Trachis.

Epicurus’s son, who walled Mitylene in and took its surrender on terms — promising not to kill anyone until Athens had answered, and keeping it. ## modern-en · theaenetus · 9:19

The same winter the Plataeans, still being besieged by the Peloponnesians and Boeotians, distressed by the failure of their provisions and seeing no hope of relief from Athens or any other means of safety, formed a scheme with the Athenians besieged with them to escape, if possible, by forcing their way over the enemy’s walls. The plan was suggested by Theaenetus, son of Tolmides, a soothsayer, and Eupompides, son of Daimachus, one of their generals. At first all were to take part; afterwards half hung back, thinking the risk too great. About two hundred and twenty, however, voluntarily persisted in the attempt, which was carried out as follows. Ladders were made to match the height of the enemy’s wall, which they measured by the layers of bricks—the side facing them not being thoroughly whitewashed. The bricks were counted by many men at once; some might miss the right number, but most would hit it, especially as they counted over and over again, and were close enough to the wall to see it well enough for their purpose. The length needed for the ladders was thus calculated from the breadth of a brick.

Tolmides’s son, a soothsayer, who with Eupompides thought of the escape over the Peloponnesian wall at Plataea.

## modern-en · ammias · 9:21

Such was the structure of the wall by which the Plataeans were blockaded. When their preparations were complete, they waited for a stormy night of wind and rain, with no moon, and then set out, guided by the authors of the enterprise. First they crossed the ditch that ran round the town; then they reached the enemy’s wall unnoticed by the sentinels, who could not see them in the darkness or hear them, since the wind drowned out the noise of their approach with its roar. They also kept a good distance from one another, so as not to be betrayed by the clash of their weapons. They were lightly equipped, with only the left foot shod, to keep them from slipping in the mud. They came up to the battlements at one of the intermediate spaces where they knew them to be unguarded. The men carrying the ladders went first and planted them; next twelve light-armed soldiers, with only a dagger and a breastplate, mounted, led by Ammias, son of Coroebus, who was the first on the wall; his followers got up after him and went six to each of the towers. After these came another party of light troops armed with spears, whose shields—so that they could climb more easily—were carried by men behind, who would hand them up when they faced the enemy. After a good many had mounted, they were discovered by the sentinels in the towers, by the noise of a tile knocked down by one of the Plataeans as he laid hold of the battlements. The alarm was instantly given, and the troops rushed to the wall, not knowing the nature of the danger because of the dark night and stormy weather. The Plataeans in the town had also chosen that moment to make a sortie against the Peloponnesian wall on the side opposite to where their men were getting over, in order to divert the besiegers’ attention. So the besiegers stayed distracted at their various posts, none venturing to leave his station to give help, and at a loss to guess what was happening. Meanwhile the three hundred set aside for emergencies went outside the wall in the direction of the alarm. Fire-signals of an attack were also raised toward Thebes; but the Plataeans in the town at once displayed a number of others, prepared in advance for this very purpose, in order to render the enemy’s signals unintelligible and to prevent his friends from getting a true picture of what was happening and coming to his aid before their comrades who had gone out had made good their escape and reached safety.

Coroebus’s son, first up the ladder and first on the Peloponnesian wall, at the head of twelve light-armed men with a dagger and a breastplate each.

## modern-en · androcrates · 9:23

Starting from the ditch, the Plataeans went all together along the road leading to Thebes, keeping the chapel of the hero Androcrates on their right, on the principle that the last road the Peloponnesians would suspect them of taking would be the one toward their enemies’ country. Indeed they could see the pursuers with torches on the Athens road toward Cithaeron and Druoskephalai, or Oakheads. After going a little more than half a mile along the Thebes road, the Plataeans turned off and took the road leading to the mountain, to Erythrae and Hysiae, and reaching the hills made good their escape to Athens, two hundred and twelve men in all. Some had turned back into the town before getting over the wall, and one archer was taken prisoner at the outer ditch. The Peloponnesians meanwhile gave up the pursuit and returned to their posts. The Plataeans in the town, knowing nothing of what had happened, and informed by those who had turned back that not a single man had escaped, sent out a herald as soon as it was day to make a truce for the recovery of the dead bodies; then, learning the truth, they desisted. In this way the Plataean party got over and were saved.

The hero whose chapel the escaping Plataeans kept on their right, taking the Thebes road because it was the last one the pursuers would think of.

## modern-en · salaethus · 9:24

Toward the close of the same winter, Salaethus, a Lacedaemonian, was sent out in a galley from Lacedaemon to Mitylene. Going by sea to Pyrrha, and from there overland, he passed along the bed of a torrent where the line of circumvallation could be crossed, and so entered Mitylene unnoticed and told the magistrates that Attica would certainly be invaded, and the forty ships intended to relieve them would arrive, and that he had been sent on to announce this and to oversee matters generally. The Mitylenians on this took courage and gave up the idea of treating with the Athenians. So this winter ended, and with it the fourth year of the war that Thucydides was the historian of.

The Lacedaemonian who got into Mitylene along a torrent bed, told them the fleet was coming, and stopped them treating with Athens — then armed the commons for a sortie, and lost the city the moment they had weapons in their hands. Found in hiding, sent to Athens and killed at once, though he offered to get the Peloponnesians away from Plataea.

## modern-en · cleomenes-commander · 9:25

The next summer the Peloponnesians sent off the forty-two ships for Mitylene, under Alcidas, their high admiral, while they themselves and their allies invaded Attica—their object being to distract the Athenians by a double movement, and so make it harder for them to act against the fleet sailing to Mitylene. The commander in this invasion was Cleomenes, in place of King Pausanias, son of Pleistoanax, his nephew, who was still a minor. Not content with laying waste whatever had grown back in the parts they had previously devastated, the invaders now extended their ravages to lands passed over in earlier incursions; so this invasion was felt by the Athenians more severely than any except the second. The enemy stayed on and on until they had overrun most of the country, expecting to hear from Lesbos of something achieved by their fleet, which they thought must by now have got across. However, since they did not get any of the results they expected, and their provisions began to run short, they retreated and dispersed to their various cities.

Who led the invasion of Attica in place of King Pausanias, his nephew, who was still a minor. Not the Cleomenes who drove the accursed out of Athens.

## modern-en · itamenes · 9:33

On his way back along shore, he touched at, among other places, Notium, the port of Colophon, where the Colophonians had settled after the upper town was captured by Itamenes and the barbarians—who had been called in by certain individuals in a party quarrel. The capture of the town took place about the time of the second Peloponnesian invasion of Attica. The refugees, after settling at Notium, again split into factions, one of which called in Arcadian and barbarian mercenaries from Pissuthnes and, entrenching them in a quarter apart, formed a new community with the Median party of the Colophonians who had joined them from the upper town. Their opponents had retired into exile and now called in Paches, who invited Hippias, the commander of the Arcadians in the fortified quarter, to a parley, on condition that, if they could not agree, he would be put back safe and sound in the fortification. However, when Hippias came out to him, he put him in custody, though not in chains, and suddenly attacked and took by surprise the fortification, putting the Arcadians and the barbarians found inside it to the sword. Afterwards he took Hippias into it as he had promised, and, as soon as he was inside, seized him and shot him down. Paches then handed Notium over to the Colophonians not of the Median party; settlers were afterwards sent out from Athens, and the place was colonised under Athenian laws, after collecting all the Colophonians found in any of the cities.

Who took the upper town of Colophon with the barbarians, having been called in by one party in a quarrel.

## modern-en · cleon · 9:35

On the arrival of the prisoners with Salaethus, the Athenians at once put the latter to death, although he offered, among other things, to procure the withdrawal of the Peloponnesians from Plataea, which was still under siege. After deliberating about what to do with the others, in the fury of the moment they decided to put to death not only the prisoners at Athens but the entire adult male population of Mitylene, and to enslave the women and children. It was remarked that Mitylene had revolted without being subjected to the empire like the rest; and what most swelled the wrath of the Athenians was the fact that the Peloponnesian fleet had ventured over to Ionia to support her, a fact taken to argue a long-meditated rebellion. They accordingly sent a galley to communicate the decree to Paches, with orders to lose no time in dispatching the Mitylenians. The next day brought repentance with it, and reflection on the horrid cruelty of a decree that condemned a whole city to the fate deserved only by the guilty. As soon as the Mitylenian ambassadors at Athens and their Athenian supporters perceived this, they moved the authorities to put the question to the vote again. The authorities consented all the more readily because they could plainly see that most of the citizens wanted someone to give them the chance to reconsider. An assembly was therefore at once called, and after much expression of opinion on both sides, Cleon, son of Cleaenetus—the same man who had carried the previous motion to put the Mitylenians to death, the most violent man at Athens and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons—came forward again and spoke as follows:

Cleaenetus’s son, the most violent man at Athens and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons, who carried the decree to kill every adult male in Mitylene and enslave the rest, and defended it the next day: a democracy is incapable of empire, your empire is a despotism, pity and sentiment and indulgence are the three failings most fatal to it, and the penalty of rebellion must be death. He lost the second vote by a show of hands that was almost equal, and got the thousand prisoners killed instead.

## modern-en · diodotus · 9:40

Such were the words of Cleon. After him Diodotus, son of Eucrates, who in the previous assembly had also spoken most strongly against putting the Mitylenians to death, came forward and spoke as follows:

Eucrates’s son, who answered Cleon by refusing to argue about guilt at all: the question is not justice but the interest of Athens, and no penalty yet invented has ever stopped men from taking a risk they have set their minds on — so killing the Mitylenian commons, who had surrendered the town the moment they got arms, would only teach every future rebel to hold out to the last. His motion carried, and the second galley beat the first by the length of a meal eaten at the oar.

## modern-en · mitylenians · 9:1

Immediately after the Peloponnesian invasion, all of Lesbos except Methymna revolted from the Athenians. The Lesbians had wished to revolt even before the war, but the Lacedaemonians would not receive them; and even now, when they did revolt, they were forced to do so sooner than they had intended. They were waiting until the moles for their harbours, and the ships and walls under construction, should be finished, and for the arrival of archers, corn, and other things they were fetching from the Pontus. But the Tenedians, with whom they were at enmity, the Methymnians, and certain factious men in Mitylene itself who were proxenoi of Athens, informed the Athenians that the Mitylenians were forcibly uniting the island under their rule, and that the preparations they were so busy with had all been concerted with the Boeotians—their kindred—and with the Lacedaemonians, with a view to revolt; and that unless the Athenians intervened at once, Athens would lose Lesbos.

Who wanted to revolt before the war and were refused, and then had to do it before their walls and moles and archers were ready. They told the allies at Olympia that fear, not friendship, had kept them in the Athenian alliance, and that the liberty of attacking being always Athens’s, the liberty of defending should be theirs. Starved out, they were sentenced to death in one assembly and reprieved in the next by a handful of votes.

While these envoys, having reached Lacedaemon after a difficult journey across the open sea, were negotiating for help to be sent them, the ambassadors from Athens returned having achieved nothing. Afterwards he took Hippias into it as he had promised, and, as soon as he was inside, seized him and shot him down. ## modern-en · nicias-niceratus · 10:0

During the same summer, after the reduction of Lesbos, the Athenians under Nicias, son of Niceratus, made an expedition against the island of Minoa, which lies off Megara and was used as a fortified post by the Megarians, who had built a tower on it. Nicias wanted to enable the Athenians to keep up their blockade from this nearer station instead of from Budorum and Salamis, to stop the Peloponnesian galleys and privateers from sailing out unobserved from the island, as they had been in the habit of doing, and at the same time to prevent anything from coming into Megara. Accordingly, after taking two towers projecting on the side of Nisaea by means of engines from the sea, and clearing the entrance into the channel between the island and the shore, he next set about cutting off all communication by building a wall on the mainland at the point where a bridge across a marsh enabled reinforcements to be thrown into the island, which was not far from the continent. A few days were enough to accomplish this. He afterwards raised some works on the island as well, and leaving a garrison there, departed with his forces.

Niceratus’s son, who took Minoa off Megara so that the blockade could be kept from a nearer station, and led sixty ships against Melos and the Locrian seaboard.

## modern-en · astymachus · 10:1

About the same time in this summer, the Plataeans, now without provisions and unable to hold out under the siege, surrendered to the Peloponnesians in the following way. An assault had been made on the wall, which the Plataeans were unable to repel. The Lacedaemonian commander, seeing their weakness, did not want to take the place by storm. His instructions from Lacedaemon had been framed so that, if at some future date peace should be made with Athens and they should agree each to restore the places taken in the war, Plataea might be considered to have come over voluntarily and not be included in the list. He accordingly sent a herald to ask if they were willing to surrender the town to the Lacedaemonians voluntarily and accept them as their judges, with the understanding that the guilty would be punished, but no one without due process. The Plataeans were now in the last stage of weakness, and as soon as the herald had delivered his message, they surrendered the town. The Peloponnesians fed them for some days until the judges from Lacedaemon, who were five in number, arrived. On their arrival no charge was put forward; they simply called up the Plataeans and asked whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in the war then in progress. The Plataeans asked leave to speak at greater length, and deputed two of their number to represent them: Astymachus, son of Asopolaus, and Lacon, son of Aeimnestus, proxenus of the Lacedaemonians, who came forward and spoke as follows:

Asopolaus’s son, one of the two Plataeans deputed to answer the five Lacedaemonian judges — who put one question and no charge, and asked it again of each man before taking him out and killing him.

## modern-en · peithias · 10:20

The Corcyraean revolution began with the return of the prisoners taken in the sea-fights off Epidamnus. The Corinthians had released these men, nominally on the security of eight hundred talents put up by their proxeni, but in reality on their undertaking to bring Corcyra over to Corinth. These men set to work canvassing each of the citizens and intriguing to detach the city from Athens. On the arrival of an Athenian and a Corinthian vessel, with envoys on board, a conference was held in which the Corcyraeans voted to remain allies of the Athenians according to their agreement, but to be friends of the Peloponnesians, as they had been before. Meanwhile, the returned prisoners brought Peithias, a volunteer proxenus of the Athenians and leader of the commons, to trial on the charge of enslaving Corcyra to Athens. Acquitted, he retorted by charging five of the wealthiest of their number with cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous, the legal penalty being a stater for each stake. They were convicted, and the amount of the penalty being very large, they seated themselves as suppliants in the temples to be allowed to pay it by instalments. But Peithias, who was one of the senate, persuaded that body to enforce the law; on which the accused, made desperate by the law, and also learning that Peithias intended, while still a member of the senate, to persuade the people to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with Athens, banded together, armed with daggers, and suddenly bursting into the senate, killed Peithias and sixty others — senators and private citizens. Only a few of Peithias's party took refuge in the Athenian galley, which had not yet sailed.

A volunteer proxenus of Athens and leader of the commons at Corcyra, acquitted on a charge of enslaving the city and answering it by prosecuting five rich men for cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous. They came into the senate house with daggers and killed him and sixty others.

## modern-en · nicostratus · 10:25

The next day the Athenian general Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenian heavy infantry. He at once tried to bring about a settlement and persuaded the two parties to agree to bring to trial ten of the ringleaders — who promptly fled — while the rest were to live in peace, coming to terms with each other and entering into a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians. This arranged, he was about to sail away when the leaders of the commons induced him to leave them five of his ships, so as to make their adversaries less inclined to make a move, while they would man and send with him an equal number of their own. He had no sooner consented than they began enrolling their enemies for the ships; and these, fearing that they might be sent off to Athens, seated themselves as suppliants in the temple of the Dioscuri. An attempt by Nicostratus to reassure them and persuade them to rise proved unsuccessful, and the commons, taking this as a pretext, armed themselves, alleging the refusal of their adversaries to sail with them as proof of the hollowness of their intentions. They took their arms out of their houses and would have killed some whom they fell in with, if Nicostratus had not prevented it. The rest of the party, seeing what was going on, seated themselves as suppliants in the temple of Hera, no fewer than four hundred in number; until the commons, fearing they might adopt some desperate resolution, induced them to rise and conveyed them over to the island in front of the temple, where provisions were sent across to them.

Diitrephes’s son, who came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenians and very nearly settled Corcyra: he got both parties to agree to try ten ringleaders, stopped the commons from killing men in the street, and persuaded four hundred suppliants out of the temple of Hera — and then sailed on.

## modern-en · laches · 10:36

At the close of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships under the command of Laches, son of Melanopus, and Charoeades, son of Euphiletus, to Sicily, where the Syracusans and Leontines were at war. The Syracusans had for allies all the Dorian cities except Camarina — these had been included in the Lacedaemonian confederacy from the start of the war, though they had not taken any active part in it. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians were for the Syracusans, the Rhegians for their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens and appealed to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin to persuade the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality to prevent the exportation of Sicilian corn to the Peloponnese and to test the possibility of bringing Sicily into subjection. Accordingly they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.

Melanopus’s son, who took twenty ships to Sicily with Charoeades, was left in sole command when Charoeades was killed, took Mylae and Messina, and was relieved by Pythodorus.

## modern-en · camarinaeans · 13:23

Such were the words of Hermocrates. The Sicilians took his advice and came to an understanding among themselves to end the war, each keeping what they had—the Camarinaeans taking Morgantina at a price fixed to be paid to the Syracusans. The allies of the Athenians called in the officers in command and told them that they were going to make peace and that they would be included in the treaty. The generals consenting, the peace was concluded, and the Athenian fleet afterwards sailed away from Sicily. On their arrival at Athens, the Athenians banished Pythodorus and Sophocles, and fined Eurymedon, on the charge of having taken bribes to depart when they might have subdued Sicily. So thoroughly had the present prosperity persuaded the citizens that nothing could withstand them, and that they could achieve what was possible and impracticable alike, with means ample or inadequate, it mattered not. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians were for the Syracusans, the Rhegians for their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens and appealed to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin to persuade the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality to prevent the exportation of Sicilian corn to the Peloponnese and to test the possibility of bringing Sicily into subjection. Accordingly they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.

Of Italy, who were for their Leontine kinsmen, and whose town the Athenians made their base.

## modern-en · agis · 11:2

The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies set out to invade Attica under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus. They got as far as the Isthmus, but with numerous earthquakes occurring, they turned back without invading. About the same time as these earthquakes were so frequent, the sea at Orobiae in Euboea retreated from the existing line of coast and then returned in a huge wave, swept over a great part of the town, and withdrew, leaving some of it still under water; what was once land is now sea. Those of the inhabitants who could not run up to higher ground in time perished. A similar inundation happened at Atalanta, the island off the Opuntian Locrian coast, carrying away part of the Athenian fort and wrecking one of two ships drawn up on the beach. At Peparethus too the sea retreated a little, but no flood followed; an earthquake threw down part of the wall, the town hall, and a few other buildings. The cause of this phenomenon, in my opinion, must be sought in the earthquake. At the point where its shock has been most violent, the sea is driven back, and then, recoiling suddenly with redoubled force, causes the inundation. Without an earthquake I do not see how such a thing could happen.

Archidamus’s son, who brought the army as far as the Isthmus and turned back without invading because of the earthquakes.

## modern-en · demosthenes · 11:4

The same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese under Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Procles, son of Theodorus, and sixty more, with two thousand heavy infantry, against Melos under Nicias, son of Niceratus. They wanted to reduce the Melians, who, although islanders, refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy. The devastation of their land did not bring them to terms, so the fleet weighed from Melos and sailed to Oropus in the territory of Graea. Landing at nightfall, the heavy infantry started at once from the ships by land for Tanagra in Boeotia, where they were met, by prearranged signal, by the whole levy from Athens, under Hipponicus, son of Callias, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. They encamped, and after spending that day ravaging the territory of Tanagra, stayed there for the night. The next day, after defeating those of the Tanagraeans who came out against them and some Thebans who had come up to help them, they took some arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew — the troops to the city, the rest to the ships. Nicias, with his sixty ships, coasted along the shore, ravaged the Locrian seaboard, and so returned home.

Alcisthenes’s son. Talked by the Messenians into invading Aetolia against the Acarnanians’ advice, he pushed on without waiting for his Locrian darters, lost his archers’ captain and then his guide, and watched a hundred and twenty Athenian hoplites — by far the best men of the city to fall in the war — die in trackless gullies and in a wood the Aetolians burned around them. He stayed at Naupactus afraid to face Athens; and then saved Naupactus, hid four hundred men in a hollow road at Olpae, broke Eurylochus’s wing from behind, and destroyed the Ambraciot relief at Idomene at dawn by putting Messenians in front to speak Doric to the sentries.

## modern-en · tisamenus · 11:5

About this time the Lacedaemonians founded their colony of Heraclea in Trachis, with this object in view. The Malians form three tribes in all — the Paralians, the Hiereans, and the Trachinians. The Trachinians, having suffered severely in a war with their neighbours the Oetaeans, at first intended to put themselves under Athens; but afterwards, fearing they would not find with her the security they sought, they sent to Lacedaemon, having chosen Tisamenus as their ambassador. The Dorians, from the mother country of the Lacedaemonians, joined this embassy with the same request, since they too were suffering from the same enemy. After hearing them, the Lacedaemonians decided to send out the colony, both to help the Trachinians and Dorians and because they thought the proposed town would lie conveniently for the war against the Athenians. A fleet might be readied there against Euboea, with the advantage of a short crossing to the island; and the town would also be useful as a station on the road to Thrace. In short, everything made the Lacedaemonians eager to found the place. After first consulting the god at Delphi and getting a favourable answer, they sent off the colonists, Spartans and Perioeci, also inviting any of the rest of the Hellenes who wished to join, except Ionians, Achaeans, and certain other peoples. Three Lacedaemonians led as founders of the colony — Leon, Alcidas, and Damagon. With the settlement made, they freshly fortified the city, now called Heraclea, about four and a half miles from Thermopylae and two and a quarter from the sea, and began building docks, closing the side toward Thermopylae just at the pass itself, so that they could be easily defended.

The ambassador the Trachinians chose to ask Lacedaemon for a colony, after suffering severely in a war with the Oetaeans.

## modern-en · hesiod · 11:10

After bivouacking with the army in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, where the poet Hesiod is said to have been killed by the people of the country, in fulfilment of an oracle that had foretold he would die at Nemea, Demosthenes set out at daybreak to invade Aetolia. The first day he took Potidania, the next Krokyle, and the third Tichium, where he halted and sent the booty back to Eupalium in Locris, having decided to push his conquests as far as the Ophionians and, if they refused to submit, to return to Naupactus and make them the object of a second expedition. Meanwhile the Aetolians had been aware of his plan from the moment it was formed, and as soon as the army invaded their country they came up in great force with all their tribes — even the most remote Ophionians, the Bomiensians, and Calliensians, who extend toward the Malian Gulf, were among them.

The poet, said to have been killed by the people of the country in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, in fulfilment of an oracle that he would die at Nemea — where Demosthenes’s army bivouacked on its way into Aetolia.

## modern-en · chromon · 11:12

Still, as long as their archers had arrows left and could use them, they held out, the light-armed Aetolians retreating before the arrows; but after the captain of the archers had been killed and his men scattered, the soldiers, worn out by the constant repetition of the same exertions and hard pressed by the Aetolians with their javelins, at last turned and fled. Falling into trackless gullies and places they did not know, they perished there; their guide, the Messenian Chromon, having unfortunately also been killed. A great many were overtaken in the pursuit by the swift-footed light-armed Aetolians and fell beneath their javelins; but most missed their way and rushed into the wood, which had no exit, and which the enemy soon set on fire and burnt round them. The Athenian army fell victims to death in every form, and went through every hardship of flight; the survivors with difficulty escaped to the sea and to Oeneon in Locris, where they had set out from. Many of the allies were killed, and about one hundred and twenty Athenian heavy infantry — not a man less, all in the prime of life. These were by far the best men of the city of Athens to fall during this war. Among the slain was also Procles, the colleague of Demosthenes. The Athenians took up their dead under truce from the Aetolians and withdrew to Naupactus, and from there sailed in their ships to Athens; Demosthenes stayed behind in Naupactus and the surrounding area, afraid to face the Athenians after the disaster.

The Messenian who guided the army in Aetolia, and whose death left it in trackless country.

## modern-en · aristotle · 11:24

The same winter the Ambraciots, as they had promised Eurylochus when they retained his army, marched out against Amphilochian Argos with three thousand heavy infantry, and invading Argive territory occupied Olpae, a stronghold on a hill near the sea, formerly fortified by the Acarnanians and used as the place of assizes for their nation, about two and three-quarters miles from the city of Argos on the seacoast. Meanwhile the Acarnanians went with part of their forces to relieve Argos, and with the rest encamped in Amphilochia at the place called Crenae, or the Wells, to watch for Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians and prevent them from passing through and joining up with the Ambraciots. They also sent for Demosthenes, the commander of the Aetolian expedition, to be their leader, and for the twenty Athenian ships cruising off the Peloponnese under the command of Aristotle, son of Timocrates, and Hierophon, son of Antimnestus. The Ambraciots at Olpae, on their part, sent a messenger to their own city begging them to come with their full levy to their aid, fearing that Eurylochus’s army might not be able to push through the Acarnanians, and that they themselves might be forced to fight alone, or be unable to retreat without danger if they wished to.

Timocrates’s son, one of the two commanders of the twenty Athenian ships the Acarnanians sent for.

Meanwhile the Acarnanians went with part of their forces to relieve Argos, and with the rest encamped in Amphilochia at the place called Crenae, or the Wells, to watch for Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians and prevent them from passing through and joining up with the Ambraciots. They also sent for Demosthenes, the commander of the Aetolian expedition, to be their leader, and for the twenty Athenian ships cruising off the Peloponnese under the command of Aristotle, son of Timocrates, and Hierophon, son of Antimnestus. The Ambraciots at Olpae, on their part, sent a messenger to their own city begging them to come with their full levy to their aid, fearing that Eurylochus’s army might not be able to push through the Acarnanians, and that they themselves might be forced to fight alone, or be unable to retreat without danger if they wished to.

Hierophon’s father.

## modern-en · salynthius · 11:29

While the enemy was taking up his dead and hastily burying them as best he could, and those who had gained permission were secretly arranging their retreat, word was brought to Demosthenes and the Acarnanians that the Ambraciots from the city, in compliance with the first message from Olpae, were on the march with their whole levy through Amphilochia to join their countrymen at Olpae, knowing nothing of what had happened. Demosthenes prepared to march out against them with his army, and meanwhile sent on at once a strong division to seize the roads and occupy the strong positions. In the meantime the Mantineans and others included in the agreement went out under the pretence of gathering herbs and firewood and slipped off in twos and threes, picking on the way the things they had pretended to come out for, until they had gone some distance from Olpae, when they quickened their pace. The Ambraciots and others who had accompanied them in larger parties, seeing them going on, pushed on in their turn and started running to catch up. The Acarnanians at first thought all alike were going off without permission and started to chase the Peloponnesians; believing they were being betrayed, they even threw a javelin or two at some of their generals who tried to stop them and explained that leave had been granted. In the end, however, they let the Mantineans and Peloponnesians pass, and killed only the Ambraciots — though there was much dispute and difficulty in telling whether a man was an Ambraciot or a Peloponnesian. The number killed in this way was about two hundred; the rest escaped into the bordering territory of Agraea and found refuge with Salynthius, the friendly king of the Agraeans.

The friendly king of the Agraeans, with whom the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who got away from Olpae took refuge.

## modern-en · pythodorus-isolochus · 11:33

The same winter the Athenians in Sicily made a landing from their ships in the territory of Himera, in concert with the Sicels, who had invaded its borders from the interior, and also sailed to the islands of Aeolus. On their return to Rhegium they found the Athenian general Pythodorus, son of Isolochus, had come to relieve Laches in command of the fleet. The allies in Sicily had sailed to Athens and induced the Athenians to send out more ships to their aid, pointing out that the Syracusans, who already had control of the land, were making efforts to put together a navy, to avoid being any longer kept off the sea by a few ships. The Athenians proceeded to man forty ships to send them, thinking the war in Sicily would thus be ended sooner, and also wanting to give their navy practice. One of the generals, Pythodorus, was accordingly sent out with a few ships; Sophocles, son of Sostratides, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles, were to follow with the main body. Meanwhile Pythodorus had taken command of Laches’ ships, and toward the end of winter sailed against the Locrian fort that Laches had previously taken, and returned after being defeated in battle by the Locrians.

Isolochus’s son, sent out to relieve Laches in Sicily, and beaten by the Locrians at the fort Laches had taken. Not the archon of the year the war began.

## modern-en · hephaestus · 11:1

The same winter the Athenians in Sicily and the Rhegians, with thirty ships, made an expedition against the islands of Aeolus, which cannot be invaded in summer because of the lack of water. These islands are held by the Liparaeans, a Cnidian colony, who live in one of them — Lipara, which is not large — and from this as their headquarters work the rest, Didyme, Strongyle, and Hiera. On Hiera the people in those parts believe that Hephaestus has his forge, from the amount of flame they see it send out by night and the smoke by day. These islands lie off the coast of the Sicels and Messenians and were allies of the Syracusans. The Athenians laid waste their land, and as the inhabitants would not submit, sailed back to Rhegium. So the winter ended, and with it the fifth year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.

Whose forge the people of those parts believe to be on Hiera, from the flame the island sends out by night and the smoke by day.

## modern-en · melians · 11:4

The same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese under Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Procles, son of Theodorus, and sixty more, with two thousand heavy infantry, against Melos under Nicias, son of Niceratus. They wanted to reduce the Melians, who, although islanders, refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy. The devastation of their land did not bring them to terms, so the fleet weighed from Melos and sailed to Oropus in the territory of Graea. Landing at nightfall, the heavy infantry started at once from the ships by land for Tanagra in Boeotia, where they were met, by prearranged signal, by the whole levy from Athens, under Hipponicus, son of Callias, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. They encamped, and after spending that day ravaging the territory of Tanagra, stayed there for the night. The next day, after defeating those of the Tanagraeans who came out against them and some Thebans who had come up to help them, they took some arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew — the troops to the city, the rest to the ships. Nicias, with his sixty ships, coasted along the shore, ravaged the Locrian seaboard, and so returned home.

Islanders who refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy, and whose land was devastated without bringing them to terms.

## modern-en · malians · 11:5

About this time the Lacedaemonians founded their colony of Heraclea in Trachis, with this object in view. The Malians form three tribes in all — the Paralians, the Hiereans, and the Trachinians. The Trachinians, having suffered severely in a war with their neighbours the Oetaeans, at first intended to put themselves under Athens; but afterwards, fearing they would not find with her the security they sought, they sent to Lacedaemon, having chosen Tisamenus as their ambassador. The Dorians, from the mother country of the Lacedaemonians, joined this embassy with the same request, since they too were suffering from the same enemy. After hearing them, the Lacedaemonians decided to send out the colony, both to help the Trachinians and Dorians and because they thought the proposed town would lie conveniently for the war against the Athenians. A fleet might be readied there against Euboea, with the advantage of a short crossing to the island; and the town would also be useful as a station on the road to Thrace. In short, everything made the Lacedaemonians eager to found the place. After first consulting the god at Delphi and getting a favourable answer, they sent off the colonists, Spartans and Perioeci, also inviting any of the rest of the Hellenes who wished to join, except Ionians, Achaeans, and certain other peoples. Three Lacedaemonians led as founders of the colony — Leon, Alcidas, and Damagon. With the settlement made, they freshly fortified the city, now called Heraclea, about four and a half miles from Thermopylae and two and a quarter from the sea, and began building docks, closing the side toward Thermopylae just at the pass itself, so that they could be easily defended.

Three tribes in all — the Paralians, the Hiereans and the Trachinians.

## modern-en · apodotians · 11:8

Demosthenes, however, had meanwhile been persuaded by the Messenians that this was a fine opportunity, with so large an army assembled, to attack the Aetolians, who were not only the enemies of Naupactus, but whose reduction would also make it easy to gain the rest of that part of the mainland for the Athenians. The Aetolian nation, although numerous and warlike, lived in unwalled villages scattered far apart and had nothing but light arms; according to the Messenians, they could be subdued without much difficulty before reinforcements could arrive. The plan they recommended was to attack first the Apodotians, then the Ophionians, and after them the Eurytanians, who are the largest tribe in Aetolia and speak, it is said, an extremely difficult language and eat their flesh raw. Once these were subdued, the rest would easily come in.

The Aetolian tribe the Messenians told Demosthenes to attack first.

## modern-en · bomiensians · 11:10

After bivouacking with the army in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, where the poet Hesiod is said to have been killed by the people of the country, in fulfilment of an oracle that had foretold he would die at Nemea, Demosthenes set out at daybreak to invade Aetolia. The first day he took Potidania, the next Krokyle, and the third Tichium, where he halted and sent the booty back to Eupalium in Locris, having decided to push his conquests as far as the Ophionians and, if they refused to submit, to return to Naupactus and make them the object of a second expedition. Meanwhile the Aetolians had been aware of his plan from the moment it was formed, and as soon as the army invaded their country they came up in great force with all their tribes — even the most remote Ophionians, the Bomiensians, and Calliensians, who extend toward the Malian Gulf, were among them.

The most remote of the Ophionians, who extend toward the Malian gulf.

## modern-en · amphissians · 11:15

After the army had assembled at Delphi, Eurylochus sent a herald to the Ozolian Locrians, since the road to Naupactus lay through their territory and he had also conceived the idea of detaching them from Athens. His chief supporters in Locris were the Amphissians, alarmed at the hostility of the Phocians. They were the first to give hostages themselves and persuaded the rest to do the same out of fear of the invading army — first their neighbours the Myonians, who held the most difficult of the passes, and after them the Ipnians, Messapians, Tritaeans, Chalaeans, Tolophonians, Hessians, and Oeanthians, all of whom joined the expedition. The Olpaeans contented themselves with giving hostages without joining the invasion, while the Hyaeans refused to do either, until the capture of Polis, one of their villages.

Eurylochus’s chief supporters in Ozolian Locris, alarmed at the hostility of the Phocians, who gave hostages first and talked the rest into it.

## modern-en · epitadas · 12:7

On the return of the Peloponnesians from Attica, the Spartans themselves and the nearest of the Perioeci at once set out for Pylos, the other Lacedaemonians following more slowly, since they had just come in from another campaign. Word was also sent round the Peloponnese to come up as quickly as possible to Pylos. The sixty Peloponnesian ships were summoned from Corcyra, and being dragged by their crews across the isthmus of Leucas, passed unnoticed by the Athenian squadron at Zacynthus and reached Pylos, where the land forces had arrived before them. Before the Peloponnesian fleet sailed in, Demosthenes found time to send out, unobserved, two ships to inform Eurymedon and the Athenians on board the fleet at Zacynthus of the danger to Pylos and to summon them to his assistance. While the ships hastened on their voyage in obedience to Demosthenes’ orders, the Lacedaemonians prepared to assault the fort by land and sea, hoping easily to capture a work built in haste and held by a feeble garrison. Meanwhile, expecting the Athenian ships to arrive from Zacynthus, they intended, if they failed to take the place first, to block the entrances to the harbour to keep them from anchoring inside it. The island of Sphacteria, stretching in a line close in front of the harbour, both makes the harbour safe and narrows its entrances, leaving a passage for two ships on the side nearest Pylos and the Athenian fortifications, and for eight or nine on the side nearest the rest of the mainland. The rest of the island was entirely covered with wood and trackless, since uninhabited, and about one mile and five furlongs in length. The Lacedaemonians meant to close the inlets with a line of ships placed close together, prows turned toward the sea. Meanwhile, fearing that the enemy might use the island as a base against them, they carried over some heavy infantry to it, stationing others along the coast. By this means the island and the mainland would both be hostile to the Athenians, who would not be able to land on either; and the shore of Pylos itself, outside the inlet toward the open sea, having no harbour, offered no point that could be used as a base to relieve their countrymen. Without a sea-fight or risk, the Lacedaemonians would in all likelihood become masters of a place taken on the spur of the moment and unprovided with provisions. With this decided, they carried over to the island the heavy infantry, drafted by lot from all the companies. Some others had crossed earlier in relief parties, but those who were left there in this final draft numbered four hundred and twenty, with their Helot attendants, commanded by Epitadas, son of Molobrus.

Molobrus’s son, who commanded the four hundred and twenty heavy infantry drafted by lot onto Sphacteria. He kept them on half rations while Helots ran corn and wine in by night for the promise of freedom, held the level middle of the island where the water was, closed ranks when the outpost was cut off, and could neither reach the light troops nor be let alone by them. He was killed before the surrender.

## modern-en · thrasymelidas · 12:10

Thus encouraged by Demosthenes, the Athenians felt more confident, and went down to meet the enemy, posting themselves along the edge of the sea. The Lacedaemonians now moved forward and at the same time assaulted the fortification with their land forces and their ships—forty-three in number—under their admiral, Thrasymelidas, son of Cratesicles, a Spartan, who made his attack just where Demosthenes expected. The Athenians thus had to defend themselves on both sides, from land and from sea. The enemy rowed up in small detachments, one relieving the other—it being impossible for many to put in at once—showing great ardour and cheering each other on, in the effort to force a passage and take the fortification. The man who most distinguished himself was Brasidas. Captain of a galley, and seeing that the captains and steersmen, struck by the difficulty of the position, hung back even where a landing seemed possible, for fear of wrecking their vessels, he shouted to them that they must never allow the enemy to fortify himself in their country for the sake of saving timber, but must shatter their ships and force a landing. He told the allies, instead of hesitating at such a moment to sacrifice their ships for Lacedaemon in return for her many benefits, to run them boldly aground, land in one way or another, and make themselves masters of the place and its garrison.

Cratesicles’s son, a Spartan, and admiral of the forty-three ships that attacked the new fort from the sea at exactly the point Demosthenes had expected.

## modern-en · demoteles · 12:32

Meanwhile the Athenians, having received warning that Camarina was about to be betrayed to the Syracusans by Archias and his party, sailed there. The Messinese took this opportunity to attack their Chalcidian neighbour, Naxos, by sea and land with all their forces. The first day they forced the Naxians to keep within their walls, and laid waste their country; the next they sailed round with their ships and laid waste their land along the river Akesines, while their land forces threatened the city. Meanwhile the Sicels came down from the high country in great numbers, to aid against the Messinese; and the Naxians, elated at the sight, and animated by a belief that the Leontines and their other Hellenic allies were coming to support them, suddenly sallied out from the town, attacked, and routed the Messinese, killing more than a thousand of them. The remainder suffered severely on their retreat home, attacked by the barbarians on the road, and most of them were cut off. The ships put in at Messina, and afterwards dispersed for their various homes. The Leontines and their allies, with the Athenians, at once turned their arms against the now weakened Messina, and attacked—the Athenians with their ships on the side of the harbour, the land forces on the side of the town. The Messinese, however, sallying out with Demoteles and some Locrians who had been left to garrison the city after the disaster, suddenly attacked and routed most of the Leontine army, killing a great number. On seeing this the Athenians landed from their ships, and falling on the Messinese in disorder chased them back into the town, and after setting up a trophy retired to Rhegium. After this the Hellenes in Sicily continued to make war on each other by land, without the Athenians.

## modern-en · styphon · 12:46

Hearing this offer, most of the Lacedaemonians lowered their shields and waved their hands to show that they accepted it. Hostilities now ceased, and a parley was held between Cleon and Demosthenes on one side, and Styphon, son of Pharax, on the other; for Epitadas, the first of the previous commanders, had been killed, and Hippagretas, the next in command, left for dead among the slain (though still alive), and so the command had devolved on Styphon according to the law, in case anything happened to his superiors. Styphon and his companions said they wished to send a herald to the Lacedaemonians on the mainland, to know what they were to do. The Athenians would not let any of them go, but themselves called for heralds from the mainland, and after questions had been carried back and forth two or three times, the last man to come over from the Lacedaemonians on the continent brought this message: “The Lacedaemonians bid you decide for yourselves, so long as you do nothing dishonourable.” On this, after consulting together, they surrendered themselves and their arms. The Athenians, after guarding them that day and night, the next morning set up a trophy on the island and got ready to sail, handing their prisoners in batches to be guarded by the captains of the galleys; and the Lacedaemonians sent a herald and took up their dead. The number of the killed and prisoners taken on the island was as follows: four hundred and twenty heavy infantry had crossed over; three hundred all but eight were taken alive to Athens; the rest were killed. About a hundred and twenty of the prisoners were Spartans. The Athenian loss was small, since the battle had not been fought at close quarters.

Pharax’s son, and third in the Spartan line of command on the island: Epitadas was dead and Hippagretas left for dead among the slain, so by law it fell to him. ## modern-en · theagenes-athens · 12:34

At Athens, meanwhile, the news that the army was in great distress, and that corn was finding its way in to the men on the island, caused no small perplexity. The Athenians began to fear that winter might come on and find them still engaged in the blockade. They saw that convoying provisions round the Peloponnese would then be impossible. The country offered no resources in itself, and even in summer they could not send round enough. The blockade of a place without harbours could no longer be kept up; and the men would either escape, by the siege being abandoned, or watch for bad weather and sail out in the boats that brought their corn. What caused still more alarm was the attitude of the Lacedaemonians, who, the Athenians thought, must feel themselves on strong ground not to send any more envoys; and they began to repent having rejected the treaty. Cleon, perceiving the disfavour with which he was regarded for having stood in the way of the convention, now said that the informants did not speak the truth; and when the messengers recommended that, if they did not believe them, some commissioners be sent to see, Cleon himself and Theagenes were chosen by the Athenians as commissioners. Aware that he would now be obliged either to say what had already been said by the men he was slandering, or be proved a liar if he said the contrary, he told the Athenians—whom he saw were not entirely disinclined for a fresh expedition—that, instead of sending and wasting their time and opportunities, if they believed what they were told, they ought to sail against the men. And pointing at Nicias, son of Niceratus, then general, whom he hated, he tauntingly said that it would be easy, if they had men for generals, to sail with a force and take those on the island; and if he himself had been in command, he would have done it.

Chosen with Cleon to go and see for himself whether the reports from Pylos were true — a commission Cleon talked the assembly out of before it could sail. Not the tyrant of Megara.

## modern-en · ulysses · 12:30

Meanwhile the Syracusans and their allies in Sicily had brought up to the squadron guarding Messina the reinforcement we left them preparing, and were carrying on the war from there, incited chiefly by the Locrians out of hatred for the Rhegians, whose territory they had invaded with all their forces. The Syracusans also wished to try their fortune at sea, seeing that the Athenians had only a few ships actually at Rhegium, and hearing that the main fleet meant to join them was engaged in blockading the island. A naval victory, they thought, would let them blockade Rhegium by sea and land and easily reduce it; a success that would at once place their affairs on a solid footing, since the promontory of Rhegium in Italy and Messina in Sicily are so near each other that it would be impossible for the Athenians to cruise against them and command the strait. The strait in question consists of the sea between Rhegium and Messina, at the point where Sicily comes nearest to the continent, and is the Charybdis through which the story makes Ulysses sail. The narrowness of the passage and the strength of the current that pours in from the vast Tyrrhenian and Sicilian mains have rightly given it a bad reputation.

Whom the story makes sail through the Charybdis: the strait between Rhegium and Messina, where Sicily comes nearest the continent, and where the current out of the Tyrrhenian and Sicilian mains has rightly given the narrows a bad name.

## modern-en · messinese · 12:31

In this strait the Syracusans and their allies were forced to fight, late in the day, over the passage of a boat, putting out with rather more than thirty ships against sixteen Athenian and eight Rhegian vessels. After this the Locrians retired from Rhegian territory, and the ships of the Syracusans and their allies united and came to anchor at Cape Pelorus, in Messinian territory, where their land forces joined them. The first day they forced the Naxians to keep within their walls, and laid waste their country; the next they sailed round with their ships and laid waste their land along the river Akesines, while their land forces threatened the city. Meanwhile the Sicels came down from the high country in great numbers, to aid against the Messinese; and the Naxians, elated at the sight, and animated by a belief that the Leontines and their other Hellenic allies were coming to support them, suddenly sallied out from the town, attacked, and routed the Messinese, killing more than a thousand of them. The remainder suffered severely on their retreat home, attacked by the barbarians on the road, and most of them were cut off. The ships put in at Messina, and afterwards dispersed for their various homes. The Leontines and their allies, with the Athenians, at once turned their arms against the now weakened Messina, and attacked—the Athenians with their ships on the side of the harbour, the land forces on the side of the town. The Messinese, however, sallying out with Demoteles and some Locrians who had been left to garrison the city after the disaster, suddenly attacked and routed most of the Leontine army, killing a great number. On seeing this the Athenians landed from their ships, and falling on the Messinese in disorder chased them back into the town, and after setting up a trophy retired to Rhegium. After this the Hellenes in Sicily continued to make war on each other by land, without the Athenians.

The Chalcidian people of Naxos in Sicily, kept inside their walls on the first day and out of their gates on the second: they saw the Sicels coming down from the high country, believed the Leontines were coming too, and routed the Messinese.

## modern-en · aristides-archippus · 13:8

Summer was now over. During the following winter, Aristides, son of Archippus, one of the commanders of the Athenian ships sent to collect money from the allies, arrested at Eion on the Strymon, Artaphernes, a Persian, on his way from the King to Lacedaemon. He was conducted to Athens, where the Athenians had his dispatches translated from the Assyrian script and read them. With many references to other matters, they essentially told the Lacedaemonians that the King did not know what they wanted, since of the many ambassadors they had sent him no two ever told the same story; if, however, they were willing to speak plainly, they should send him some envoys with this Persian. The Athenians afterwards sent Artaphernes back in a galley to Ephesus, and ambassadors with him, who there learned of the death of King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, which took place about that time, and so returned home.

Archippus’s son, one of the commanders of the squadron sent round to collect money from the allies. He arrested Artaphernes at Eion with the King’s dispatches on him, and afterwards helped Demodocus retake Antandrus from the Mitylenian exiles. Not Lysimachus’s son.

Hermon’s son, a Syracusan, and the most influential man at the congress of Gela. He told the Sicilians that the question before them was not their several grievances but whether there was still time to save the island; that no one should think the Dorians alone were the enemy while Chalcidian blood protected the rest, since the attack was aimed not at a nationality but at what was in Sicily, the common property of them all; and that the quickest way to be rid of the guests was to stop giving them a reason to stay. They took his advice and kept what they had.

## modern-en · hippocrates-ariphron · 13:24

The same summer the Megarians in the city, pressed by the hostilities of the Athenians, who invaded their country twice every year with all their forces, and harassed by the incursions of their own exiles at Pegae, who had been expelled in a revolution by the popular party, began to ask one another whether it would not be better to receive back their exiles, and free the town from one of its two scourges. The friends of the émigrés, perceiving the agitation, now more openly than before demanded the adoption of this proposal; and the leaders of the commons, seeing that the sufferings of the times had worn out the loyalty of their supporters, in their alarm entered into correspondence with the Athenian generals, Hippocrates, son of Ariphron, and Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and resolved to betray the town, thinking this less dangerous to themselves than the return of the party they had banished. It was accordingly arranged that the Athenians should first take the long walls extending nearly a mile from the city to the port of Nisaea, to prevent the Peloponnesians from coming to the rescue from there, where they formed the sole garrison securing the loyalty of Megara; and that after this an attempt should be made to put into their hands the upper town, which it was thought would then come over with less difficulty.

Ariphron’s son. With Demosthenes he took the long walls of Megara by an ambush at a gate that was opened every night for a smuggler’s boat on a cart; and then designed the double stroke on Boeotia — Siphae and Chaeronea handed over on an appointed day while he fortified Delium, so that the Boeotians could not unite against any of it. The days were mistaken and the plot was betrayed, and he was left to fortify the sanctuary of Apollo alone and to fight Pagondas with a mass levy that had mostly gone home. ## modern-en · enyalius · 13:25

The Athenians, after plans had been arranged between themselves and their correspondents on both words and actions, sailed by night to Minoa, the island off Megara, with six hundred heavy infantry under the command of Hippocrates, and took up position in a quarry not far off, from which bricks used to be taken for the walls; while Demosthenes, the other commander, with a detachment of Plataean light troops and another of Peripoli, placed himself in ambush in the precinct of Enyalius, which was still nearer. No one knew of it except those whose business it was to know that night. A little before daybreak, the traitors in Megara began to act. Every night for a long time back, under pretence of marauding, in order to have a means of opening the gates, they had been used—with the consent of the officer in command—to carry by night a sculling boat on a cart along the ditch to the sea, and so to sail out, bringing it back again before day on the cart, and taking it within the wall through the gates, in order, as they pretended, to baffle the Athenian blockade at Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbour. On the present occasion the cart was already at the gates, which had been opened in the usual way for the boat, when the Athenians, with whom this had been concerted, saw it and ran at top speed from the ambush in order to reach the gates before they were shut again, and while the cart was still there to keep them from being closed; their Megarian accomplices at the same moment killing the guard at the gates. The first to run in was Demosthenes with his Plataeans and Peripoli, just where the trophy now stands; and he was no sooner inside the gates than the Plataeans engaged and defeated the nearest party of Peloponnesians, who had taken the alarm and come to the rescue, and secured the gates for the approaching Athenian heavy infantry.

In whose precinct, nearer Megara than the quarry, Demosthenes lay in ambush with the Plataean light troops and the Peripoli.

## modern-en · andrians · 13:0

The same summer, immediately after these events, the Athenians made an expedition against the territory of Corinth with eighty ships and two thousand Athenian heavy infantry, and two hundred cavalry on board horse transports, accompanied by the Milesians, Andrians, and Carystians from the allies, under the command of Nicias, son of Niceratus, with two colleagues. Putting out to sea, they made land at daybreak between Chersonese and Rheitus, on the beach of the country beneath the Solygian hill—where the Dorians in old times had established themselves and made war on the Aeolian inhabitants of Corinth, and where a village now stands called Solygia. The beach where the fleet came in is about a mile and a half from the village, seven miles from Corinth, and two and a quarter from the Isthmus. The Corinthians had heard from Argos of the coming of the Athenian armament, and had all come up to the Isthmus long before, except those who lived beyond it, and five hundred who were away on garrison duty in Ambracia and Leucadia; and they were there in full force watching for the Athenians to land. The Athenians, however, gave them the slip by coming in the dark; and the Corinthians, informed by signals of the fact, left half their number at Cenchreae, in case the Athenians should march on Crommyon, and themselves marched in all haste to the rescue.

Whose contingent served under Nicias against Corinth; and whose colonies — Acanthus, Stagirus, Argilus, Sane — stand in the Thracian country Brasidas was about to walk through.

## modern-en · cytherians · 13:12

Coming to land here with their armament, the Athenians, with ten ships and two thousand Milesian heavy infantry, took the town of Scandea on the sea; with the rest of their forces, landing on the side of the island facing Malea, they marched against the lower town of Cythera, where they found all the inhabitants encamped. Lacedaemonians of the Perioeci class, on the island that took the merchantmen from Egypt and Libya and kept privateers off the one assailable stretch of the Laconian coast. A judge went over to them from Sparta every year. They held their ground a little while, capitulated to Nicias — with whom some of them had been in correspondence — and kept their lands at four talents tribute.

## modern-en · demodocus · 14:0

That same summer the Mitylenians were about to fortify Antandrus, as they had intended, when Demodocus and Aristides, the commanders of the Athenian squadron engaged in collecting subsidies, heard on the Hellespont of what was being done to the place (Lamachus, their colleague, having sailed with ten ships into the Pontus). They feared it might become a second Anaia — the place where the Samian exiles had established themselves to harass Samos, helping the Peloponnesians by sending pilots to their navy, keeping the city in agitation, and receiving all its outlaws. They accordingly gathered a force from the allies, set sail, defeated in battle the troops that came out from Antandrus to meet them, and retook the place. Not long after, Lamachus, who had sailed into the Pontus, lost his ships at anchor in the river Calex in the territory of Heraclea, when rain that had fallen in the interior brought a flood suddenly down on them; and he and his troops marched overland through the Bithynian Thracians on the Asiatic side, and arrived at Chalcedon, the Megarian colony at the mouth of the Pontus.

One of the two commanders of the Athenian money-collecting squadron, who heard on the Hellespont what was being done at Antandrus and retook the place before it could become a second Anaia.

## modern-en · ptoeodorus · 14:1

That same summer the Athenian general Demosthenes arrived at Naupactus with forty ships, immediately after the return from the Megarid. He and Hippocrates had had overtures from certain men in the cities of Boeotia who wanted to change the constitution and bring in democracy as at Athens, the chief mover in this intrigue being Ptoeodorus, a Theban exile. The seaport town of Siphae, in the bay of Crisae in Thespian territory, was to be betrayed to them by one party; Chaeronea (a dependency of what was formerly called the Minyan, now the Boeotian, Orchomenus) was to be put into their hands by another from that town, whose exiles were very active in the business, hiring men in the Peloponnese. Some Phocians were also in the plot, since Chaeronea was the frontier town of Boeotia and close to Phanotis in Phocia. Meanwhile the Athenians were to seize Delium, the sanctuary of Apollo, in the territory of Tanagra facing Euboea; and all these events were to take place at the same time on an appointed day, so that the Boeotians would be unable to unite to oppose them at Delium, since they would be detained everywhere by disturbances at home. Should the enterprise succeed, and Delium be fortified, its authors confidently expected that even if no revolution immediately followed in Boeotia, yet with these places in their hands, the country harassed by raids, and a refuge close at hand for the partisans engaged in them, things would not stay as they were; and that with the rebels supported by the Athenians and the forces of the oligarchs divided, it would be possible after a while to settle matters as they wished.

A Theban exile, and the chief mover in the plot to change the constitutions of the Boeotian cities and bring in democracy as at Athens.

## modern-en · panaerus · 14:3

About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march for the Thracian towns with seventeen hundred heavy infantry, and on arriving at Heraclea in Trachis sent on a messenger to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to escort him and his army through the country. Accordingly there came to Melitia in Achaia: Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus, and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, under whose escort he resumed his march, accompanied also by other Thessalians, including Niconidas of Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to traverse Thessaly without an escort; and throughout Hellas, for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbour's country was a delicate step. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians; indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to proceed. Even as it was, he was met on his march at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. To this his escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will: they were only friends in attendance on an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, his arms being directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war; and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and Lacedaemonians that should prevent the two nations from having access to each other's territory, he neither would nor could proceed against their wishes — he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away, and he took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. Thus, on the day he set out from Melitia, he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus; and from there to Phacium, and from there to Perrhaebia. Here his Thessalian escort turned back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of Thessaly, set him down at Dium in the dominions of Perdiccas, a Macedonian town under Mount Olympus, looking toward Thessaly.

One of the Thessalians who came to Melitia to escort Brasidas through a country whose people had always sympathised with Athens — and which, Thucydides says, he could never have crossed at all if it had not been governed by a close oligarchy.

About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march for the Thracian towns with seventeen hundred heavy infantry, and on arriving at Heraclea in Trachis sent on a messenger to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to escort him and his army through the country.
