## modern-en · arrhabaeus · 14:4

In this way Brasidas hurried through Thessaly before anyone could get ready to stop him, and reached Perdiccas and Chalcidice. The departure of the army from the Peloponnese had been procured by the Thracian towns in revolt against Athens and by Perdiccas, alarmed at Athenian successes. The Chalcidians thought they would be the first targets of an Athenian expedition, though the neighbouring towns that had not yet revolted also secretly joined in the invitation; and Perdiccas, too, had his apprehensions because of his old quarrels with the Athenians, although he was not openly at war with them, and above all wished to reduce Arrhabaeus, king of the Lyncestians. It had been the easier to get an army to leave the Peloponnese because of the ill fortune of the Lacedaemonians at the moment. The Athenian attacks on the Peloponnese, and in particular on Laconia, might, it was hoped, be diverted most effectually by harassing them in return, and by sending an army to their allies — especially as the allies were willing to maintain it and asked for it to aid them in revolting. The Lacedaemonians were also glad to have an excuse for sending some of the Helots out of the country, for fear that the present state of affairs and the occupation of Pylos might encourage them to move. Indeed, fear of their numbers and stubbornness even drove the Lacedaemonians to the action I shall now describe, their policy at all times having been governed by the need to take precautions against them. The Helots were invited by a proclamation to pick out those of their number who claimed to have distinguished themselves most against the enemy, in order that they might receive their freedom; the real object being to test them, since it was thought that those most quick to claim their freedom would be the most high-spirited and the most likely to rebel. As many as two thousand were selected accordingly, who crowned themselves and went round the temples, rejoicing in their new freedom. The Spartans, however, soon afterwards did away with them, and no one ever knew how each of them perished. The Spartans now, therefore, gladly sent seven hundred as heavy infantry with Brasidas, who recruited the rest of his force by means of money in the Peloponnese.

Bromerus’s son and king of the Lyncestian Macedonians — the neighbour Perdiccas most wanted put down, and the reason he had paid for a Peloponnesian army. Brasidas parleyed with him instead of invading, and Perdiccas cut his contribution from half the army’s keep to a third. On the second expedition the Lyncestians were beaten in the field and took to the heights; then the Illyrian mercenaries hired for Perdiccas came over to Arrhabaeus instead, and it was the Peloponnesians who had to fight their way home.

## modern-en · bromerus · 14:7

On the arrival of Brasidas and his army, Perdiccas at once set out with them and his own forces against Arrhabaeus, son of Bromerus, king of the Lyncestian Macedonians, his neighbour, with whom he had a quarrel and whom he wanted to subdue. When, however, he arrived with his army and Brasidas at the pass leading into Lyncus, Brasidas told him that before opening hostilities he wished to go and try to persuade Arrhabaeus to become an ally of Lacedaemon. Arrhabaeus had already made overtures hinting at his willingness to make Brasidas arbitrator between them, and the Chalcidian envoys accompanying Brasidas had warned him not to relieve the apprehensions of Perdiccas, so as to keep him keener in their cause. Besides, the envoys of Perdiccas had spoken at Lacedaemon of his bringing many of the surrounding places into alliance with them, so Brasidas thought he might take a larger view of the question of Arrhabaeus. Perdiccas, however, retorted that he had not brought Brasidas with him to arbitrate his quarrel, but to put down the enemies he pointed out to him; and that while he, Perdiccas, was maintaining half the army, it was a breach of faith for Brasidas to parley with Arrhabaeus. Nevertheless, Brasidas disregarded Perdiccas's wishes and held the parley in spite of him, and let himself be persuaded to lead off the army without invading the country of Arrhabaeus; after which Perdiccas, judging that faith had not been kept with him, contributed only a third instead of half of the support of the army.

Arrhabaeus’s father.

Such were the events of this summer. A mistake, however, was made in the days on which they were each to start, and Demosthenes, sailing first to Siphae with the Acarnanians and many of the allies from those parts on board, failed to accomplish anything, since the plot had been betrayed by Nicomachus, a Phocian from Phanotis, who told the Lacedaemonians, and they the Boeotians. Aeolidas’s son, Boeotarch of Thebes and commander-in-chief at Delium, and the one of the eleven who wanted to fight after the Athenians had already crossed back over the border. He told them that with a neighbour like this there is no frontier to argue about, since conquest would mean one frontier for the whole country; massed the Thebans twenty-five shields deep on the right; and when his left was breaking sent two squadrons of horse round the hill where they could not be seen, whose sudden appearance panicked the winning Athenian wing into thinking a second army had come.

## modern-en · aristagoras · 14:28

That same winter Brasidas, with his allies in the Thracian places, marched against Amphipolis, the Athenian colony on the river Strymon. A settlement on the spot where the city now stands had previously been attempted by Aristagoras the Milesian (when he fled from King Darius), but he was dislodged by the Edonians; and thirty-two years later by the Athenians, who sent thither ten thousand settlers of their own citizens, and whoever else chose to go. These were cut off at Drabescus by the Thracians. Twenty-nine years afterwards, the Athenians returned (Hagnon, son of Nicias, being sent out as leader of the colony) and drove out the Edonians, founding a town on the spot, formerly called Ennea Hodoi or Nine Ways. The base from which they started was Eion, their commercial seaport at the mouth of the river, no more than three miles from the present town, which Hagnon named Amphipolis, because the Strymon flows round it on two sides; and he built it to be conspicuous from sea and land alike, running a long wall across from river to river to complete the circumference.

The Milesian who first tried to settle the spot that became Amphipolis, when he fled from King Darius, and was dislodged by the Edonians.

## modern-en · eucles · 14:30

Brasidas's crossing was a complete surprise to the people in the town, and the capture of many of those outside, combined with the flight of the rest within the wall, produced great confusion among the citizens, especially as they did not trust one another. It is even said that if Brasidas, instead of stopping to plunder, had advanced straight against the town, he would probably have taken it. As it was, however, he established himself where he was and overran the country outside, and for the present remained inactive, vainly waiting for a demonstration on the part of his friends within. Meanwhile the party opposed to the traitors proved numerous enough to keep the gates from being immediately thrown open, and in concert with Eucles, the general who had come from Athens to defend the place, sent to the other commander in Thrace, Thucydides, son of Olorus, the author of this history, who was at the isle of Thasos, a Parian colony half a day's sail from Amphipolis, telling him to come to their relief. On receipt of this message he at once set sail with the seven ships he had with him, in order, if possible, to reach Amphipolis in time to prevent its capitulation, or in any case to save Eion.

The general sent from Athens to defend Amphipolis. He could not get the gates held, sent down the coast for Thucydides, and watched the town accept Brasidas’s terms while the citizens stopped listening to him.

After this Thucydides put everything in order at Eion to secure it against any present or future attack by Brasidas, and received those who had elected to come there from the interior according to the agreed terms. When they would not submit, he at once marched against Torone in Chalcidice, which was held by an Athenian garrison, having been invited by a few persons who were prepared to hand over the town. ## modern-en · phoenippus · 14:53

The tribe of Acamantis had the prytany, Phoenippus was secretary, Niciades chairman. Laches moved, in the name of the good luck of the Athenians, that they should conclude the armistice on the terms agreed by the Lacedaemonians and the allies. It was agreed accordingly in the popular assembly that the armistice should be for one year, beginning that very day, the fourteenth of the month of Elaphebolion; during which time ambassadors and heralds should go and come between the two countries to discuss the bases of a pacification. The generals and prytanes should call an assembly of the people, in which the Athenians should first consult on the peace, and on the mode in which the embassy for putting an end to the war should be admitted. The embassy now present should at once give the undertaking before the people to keep well and truly this truce for one year.

## modern-en · aristonymus-athens · 14:57

In the midst of his designs on the towns in question, a galley arrived with the commissioners carrying round news of the armistice — Aristonymus for the Athenians and Athenaeus for the Lacedaemonians. The troops now crossed back to Torone, and the commissioners gave Brasidas notice of the convention. All the Lacedaemonian allies in Thrace accepted what had been done; and Aristonymus made no difficulty about the rest, but finding, on counting the days, that the Scionaeans had revolted after the date of the convention, refused to include them in it. To this Brasidas earnestly objected, asserting that the revolt took place before, and would not give up the town. On Aristonymus reporting the case to Athens, the people at once prepared to send an expedition to Scione. At this, envoys arrived from Lacedaemon alleging that this would be a breach of the truce, laying claim to the town on the faith of Brasidas's assertion, and meanwhile offering to submit the question to arbitration. Arbitration, however, was what the Athenians did not choose to risk, being determined to send troops at once to the place, and furious at the idea of even the islanders now daring to revolt in a vain reliance on the power of the Lacedaemonians by land. Besides, the facts of the revolt were rather as the Athenians contended, the Scionaeans having revolted two days after the convention. Cleon accordingly succeeded in carrying a decree to reduce and put to death the Scionaeans; and the Athenians used the leisure they now enjoyed to prepare for the expedition.

The Athenian commissioner who carried the armistice round the Thracian towns. He made no difficulty about the rest, but counted the days, found that Scione had gone over after the convention, and refused to include it — on which Brasidas said flatly that the revolt had come first and would not give the town up. The facts were rather as the Athenians contended. Not Euphamidas’s father.

## modern-en · polydamidas · 14:58

Meanwhile Mende revolted, a town in Pallene and a colony of the Eretrians, and was received without scruple by Brasidas, in spite of its having evidently come over during the armistice, on account of certain infringements of the truce alleged by him against the Athenians. This audacity of Mende was partly caused by seeing Brasidas forward in the matter and by the conclusions drawn from his refusal to betray Scione; and besides, the conspirators in Mende were few and, as I have already indicated, had carried on their practices too long not to fear detection for themselves and not to wish to force the inclination of the multitude. This news made the Athenians more furious than ever, and they at once made preparations against both towns. Brasidas, expecting their arrival, conveyed away to Olynthus in Chalcidice the women and children of the Scionaeans and Mendaeans, and sent over to them five hundred Peloponnesian heavy infantry and three hundred Chalcidian targeteers, all under the command of Polydamidas.

The commander Brasidas sent over to Scione and Mende with five hundred Peloponnesian heavy infantry and three hundred Chalcidian targeteers. Inside Mende he drew up the piled arms for a sortie, was answered factiously by one of the popular party, and dragged the man by the arm and knocked him about — which put the commons into their arms and lost him the town in an afternoon.

## modern-en · ischagoras · 14:67

While the investment of Scione was in progress, Perdiccas sent a herald to the Athenian generals and made peace with the Athenians, out of spite against Brasidas for the retreat from Lyncus — from which moment indeed he had begun to negotiate. The Lacedaemonian Ischagoras was just then on the point of starting with an army overland to join Brasidas; and Perdiccas, being now required by Nicias to give some proof of the sincerity of his reconciliation to the Athenians, and being himself no longer willing to let the Peloponnesians into his country, set in motion his friends in Thessaly, with whose chief men he always took care to have relations, and so effectually stopped the army and its preparation that they did not even try the Thessalians. Ischagoras himself, however, with Ameinias and Aristeus, succeeded in reaching Brasidas; they had been commissioned by the Lacedaemonians to inspect the state of affairs, and brought out from Sparta (in violation of all precedent) some of their young men to put in command of the towns, to guard against their being entrusted to persons on the spot. Brasidas accordingly placed Clearidas, son of Cleonymus, in Amphipolis, and Pasitelidas, son of Hegesander, in Torone.

The Lacedaemonian whose overland army for Brasidas was stopped before it started, by Perdiccas setting his friends in Thessaly in motion. He got through himself with Ameinias and Aristeus to see how matters stood, and brought out from Sparta — in violation of all precedent — young men to be put in command of the towns, rather than leave them to persons on the spot.

Accordingly there came to Melitia in Achaia: Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus, and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, under whose escort he resumed his march, accompanied also by other Thessalians, including Niconidas of Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to traverse Thessaly without an escort; and throughout Hellas, for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbour's country was a delicate step. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians; indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to proceed. Even as it was, he was met on his march at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. To this his escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will: they were only friends in attendance on an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, his arms being directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war; and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and Lacedaemonians that should prevent the two nations from having access to each other's territory, he neither would nor could proceed against their wishes — he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away, and he took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. Thus, on the day he set out from Melitia, he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus; and from there to Phacium, and from there to Perrhaebia. ## modern-en · euboeans · 14:16

“Boeotians, the idea that we ought not to give battle to the Athenians unless we came up with them inside Boeotia is one that should never have entered the head of any of us, your generals. It was to harass Boeotia that they crossed the frontier and built a fort in our country, and they are therefore, I imagine, our enemies wherever we may come up with them, and from wherever they may have come to act as enemies do. And if anyone has adopted the contrary view for reasons of safety, it is high time for him to change his mind. The party attacked, whose own country is in danger, can scarcely discuss what is prudent with the calmness of men who are in full enjoyment of what they have, and who are thinking of attacking a neighbour in order to get more. It is your national habit, in your own country or out of it, to oppose the same resistance to a foreign invader; and when that invader is Athenian, and lives on your frontier besides, it is doubly imperative to do so. As between neighbours generally, freedom means simply a determination to hold one's own; and with neighbours like these, who are trying to enslave near and far alike, there is nothing for it but to fight it out to the last. Look at the state of the Euboeans and of most of the rest of Hellas, and be convinced that others have to fight with their neighbours over this frontier or that, but that for us conquest means one frontier for the whole country, about which no dispute can be made — for they will simply come and take by force what we have. So much more have we to fear from this neighbour than from any other. Besides, people who, like the Athenians in the present instance, are tempted by pride of strength to attack their neighbours, usually march most confidently against those who keep still and only defend themselves in their own country, but think twice before they grapple with those who meet them outside their frontier and strike the first blow if opportunity offers. The Athenians have shown us this themselves: the defeat we inflicted on them at Coronea, at the time when our quarrels had allowed them to occupy the country, gave Boeotia great security to this very day. Remembering this, the old must equal their ancient exploits, and the young, the sons of the heroes of that time, must try not to disgrace their native valour. Trusting in the help of the god whose temple has been sacrilegiously fortified, and in the victims that have proved propitious in our sacrifices, we must march against the enemy and teach him that he must go and get what he wants by attacking someone who will not resist him, but that men whose glory it is always to be ready to give battle for the liberty of their own country, and never unjustly to enslave that of others, will not let him go without a struggle.”

At whose condition, and at most of the rest of Hellas, Pagondas told the Boeotians to look and be convinced.

At the close of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships under the command of Laches, son of Melanopus, and Charoeades, son of Euphiletus, to Sicily, where the Syracusans and Leontines were at war. The Syracusans had for allies all the Dorian cities except Camarina — these had been included in the Lacedaemonian confederacy from the start of the war, though they had not taken any active part in it. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians were for the Syracusans, the Rhegians for their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens and appealed to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin to persuade the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality to prevent the exportation of Sicilian corn to the Peloponnese and to test the possibility of bringing Sicily into subjection. Accordingly they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.

## modern-en · phaeax · 15:2

About the same time, Phaeax son of Erasistratus set sail with two colleagues as ambassador from Athens to Italy and Sicily. After the Athenians had left Sicily on the pacification, the Leontines had enrolled a number of new citizens, and the commons had a plan to redivide the land. The upper classes, aware of this, called in the Syracusans and expelled the commons. The commons were scattered in various directions, while the upper classes came to an agreement with the Syracusans, abandoned and laid waste their own city, and went to live in Syracuse, where they were made citizens. Afterwards some of them grew dissatisfied. They left Syracuse and occupied Phocaeae, a quarter of the town of Leontini, and Bricinniae, a strong place in Leontine territory. There, joined by most of the exiled commons, they carried on the war from these fortifications. The Athenians, hearing of this, sent Phaeax to see whether he could somehow convince their allies there and the rest of the Sicilians of the ambitious designs of Syracuse, and induce them to form a general coalition against her, and so save the commons of Leontini. Once in Sicily, Phaeax succeeded at Camarina and Agrigentum, but was rebuffed at Gela, and so did not go on to the rest, since he saw he would not succeed with them. He returned through the country of the Sicels to Catana, visiting Bricinniae on the way and encouraging its inhabitants, and then sailed back to Athens.

Erasistratus’s son, sent with two colleagues to Italy and Sicily to talk the Sicilians into a general coalition against Syracuse and so save the commons of Leontini. He succeeded at Camarina and Agrigentum, was rebuffed at Gela, and gave the rest up rather than be refused again; on the way home he made terms with the Locrian settlers he met, who were the only allies that had not come into the Sicilian peace.

## modern-en · erasistratus · 15:2

About the same time, Phaeax son of Erasistratus set sail with two colleagues as ambassador from Athens to Italy and Sicily. After the Athenians had left Sicily on the pacification, the Leontines had enrolled a number of new citizens, and the commons had a plan to redivide the land. The upper classes, aware of this, called in the Syracusans and expelled the commons. The commons were scattered in various directions, while the upper classes came to an agreement with the Syracusans, abandoned and laid waste their own city, and went to live in Syracuse, where they were made citizens. Afterwards some of them grew dissatisfied. They left Syracuse and occupied Phocaeae, a quarter of the town of Leontini, and Bricinniae, a strong place in Leontine territory. There, joined by most of the exiled commons, they carried on the war from these fortifications. The Athenians, hearing of this, sent Phaeax to see whether he could somehow convince their allies there and the rest of the Sicilians of the ambitious designs of Syracuse, and induce them to form a general coalition against her, and so save the commons of Leontini. Once in Sicily, Phaeax succeeded at Camarina and Agrigentum, but was rebuffed at Gela, and so did not go on to the rest, since he saw he would not succeed with them. He returned through the country of the Sicels to Catana, visiting Bricinniae on the way and encouraging its inhabitants, and then sailed back to Athens.

Phaeax’s father.

## modern-en · polles · 15:4

Cleon, whom we left on his voyage from Torone to Amphipolis, made Eion his base. After an unsuccessful assault on the Andrian colony of Stagirus, he took Galepsus, a colony of Thasos, by storm. He now sent envoys to Perdiccas to require his attendance with an army, as the alliance provided, and others to Thrace, to Polles, king of the Odomantians, who was to bring as many Thracian mercenaries as possible. He himself remained inactive at Eion, awaiting their arrival. Informed of this, Brasidas in turn took up a position of observation on Cerdylium, a place on high ground in Argilian territory across the river, not far from Amphipolis. It commanded a view in every direction, so that Cleon's army could not move without his seeing it; for he fully expected that Cleon, despising the small numbers of his opponent, would march against Amphipolis with the force he already had with him. At the same time Brasidas made his preparations, calling to his standard fifteen hundred Thracian mercenaries and all the Edonians, both horse and targeteers. He also had a thousand Myrcinian and Chalcidian targeteers, in addition to those in Amphipolis, and a force of heavy infantry numbering altogether about two thousand, plus three hundred Hellenic horse. Of these, fifteen hundred he had with him on Cerdylium; the rest were stationed with Clearidas in Amphipolis.

King of the Odomantians, whom Cleon asked for as many Thracian mercenaries as he could bring. Cleon was still waiting for them at Eion when his own soldiers’ grumbling forced him up to Amphipolis.

## modern-en · autocharidas · 15:10

About the same time three Lacedaemonians — Ramphias, Autocharidas, and Epicydidas — led a reinforcement of nine hundred heavy infantry to the towns in the direction of Thrace. Arriving at Heraclea in Trachis, they reorganized matters there as they thought best. While they delayed there, this battle took place, and so the summer ended.

One of the three Lacedaemonians who took nine hundred heavy infantry toward Thrace, got as far as Pierium in Thessaly, and turned back when they heard Brasidas was dead.

## modern-en · aristocles-brother-of-pleistoanax · 15:14

Now, however, after the Athenian defeat at Amphipolis and the deaths of Cleon and Brasidas — who had been the two principal opponents of peace on either side, the latter because of the success and honor war gave him, the former because he thought that, if peace were restored, his crimes would be more easily detected and his slanders less believed — the foremost candidates for power in each city desired peace more ardently than ever. These were Pleistoanax son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon, and Nicias son of Niceratus, the most successful general of his time. Nicias, while still fortunate and honored, wished to secure his good fortune, to obtain a present release from trouble for himself and his countrymen, and to hand down to posterity a name as an ever-successful statesman. He thought the way to do this was to keep out of danger and commit himself as little as possible to fortune — and that only peace made keeping out of danger possible. Pleistoanax, on his side, was attacked by his enemies over his restoration, and was regularly held up by them to the prejudice of his countrymen whenever any reverse befell them, on the grounds that his unjust restoration was the cause. The accusation was that he and his brother Aristocles had bribed the prophetess of Delphi to tell the Lacedaemonian deputations who successively arrived at the temple to bring home from abroad the seed of the demigod son of Zeus, otherwise they would have to plow with a silver plowshare. In this way, it was alleged, he had eventually induced the Lacedaemonians, in the nineteenth year of his exile in Lycaeum (where he had gone when banished on suspicion of having been bribed to retreat from Attica, and had built half his house within the sacred precinct of Zeus for fear of the Lacedaemonians), to restore him with the same dances and sacrifices with which they had instituted their kings on the first settlement of Lacedaemon. The smart of this accusation, and the thought that in peacetime no disaster could occur, and that once Lacedaemon had recovered her men there would be nothing for his enemies to take hold of (whereas while the war lasted the highest station must always bear the blame for whatever went wrong), made him ardently desire a settlement. Accordingly the winter was spent in conferences. As spring approached rapidly, the Lacedaemonians sent round orders to the cities to prepare for a fortified occupation of Attica, and held this as a sword over the Athenians to induce them to listen to their offers. At last, after many claims had been urged on either side at the conferences, a peace was agreed on the following basis. Each side was to restore its conquests, but Athens was to keep Nisaea. Her demand for Plataea was countered by the Thebans' assertion that they had acquired the place not by force or treachery, but by the voluntary adhesion of its citizens by agreement — the same, according to the Athenian account, being the history of her acquisition of Nisaea. With this settled, the Lacedaemonians summoned their allies, and when all voted for peace except the Boeotians, Corinthians, Eleans, and Megarians, who did not approve of the proceedings, they concluded the treaty and made peace, each of the contracting parties swearing to the following articles:

Pleistoanax’s brother, accused with him of bribing the prophetess at Delphi to tell every Lacedaemonian deputation that arrived to bring home the seed of the demigod son of Zeus, or else plough with a silver ploughshare. Not the polemarch who would not move his company at Mantinea.

## modern-en · pleistolas · 15:26

The treaty begins from the ephoralty of Pleistolas in Lacedaemon, on the 27th day of the month of Artemisium, and from the archonship of Alcaeus at Athens, on the 25th day of the month of Elaphebolion. Those who took the oath and poured the libations for the Lacedaemonians were Pleistoanax, Agis, Pleistolas, Damagetis, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Tellis, Alcinadas, Empedias, Menas, and Laphilus. For the Athenians: Lampon, Isthmonicus, Nicias, Laches, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, and Demosthenes.

The ephor at Lacedaemon by whose year the Peace of Nicias is dated, and one of the seventeen who swore to it.

## modern-en · arcesilaus · 16:36

When this offer was not accepted, the Eleans tried a second. Instead of restoring Lepreum, if that was objected to, the Lacedaemonians should ascend the altar of Olympian Zeus, since they were so anxious to have access to the temple, and swear before the Hellenes that they would in fact pay the fine at a later date. This too was refused. So the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple, the sacrifice, and the games, and sacrificed at home, the Lepreans being the only other Hellenes who did not attend. Still the Eleans were afraid of the Lacedaemonians sacrificing by force, and kept watch with a company of heavy-armed young men. They were also joined by a thousand Argives, the same number of Mantineans, and some Athenian cavalry who stayed at Harpina during the festival. Great fears were felt in the assembly that the Lacedaemonians might come in arms, especially after Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, a Lacedaemonian, had been scourged on the course by the umpires. The reason was that, when his horses won and the Boeotian people were proclaimed the victors because he had no right to enter, he came forward on the course and crowned the charioteer, to show that the chariot was his. After this incident, everyone was more afraid than before, and confidently expected a disturbance. The Lacedaemonians, however, kept quiet and let the festival pass by, as we have seen. After the Olympic games, the Argives and the allies went to Corinth to invite her to come over to them. There they found some Lacedaemonian envoys, and a long discussion took place, which in the end came to nothing, as an earthquake occurred and they dispersed to their various homes.

Lichas’s father.

Expelled from their own island by Athens, which had concluded that some old offence at the time of their consecration was the flaw in the purification; they were given Atramyttium in Asia by Pharnaces, and brought back two years later on the command of the god at Delphi.

When they would not submit, he at once marched against Torone in Chalcidice, which was held by an Athenian garrison, having been invited by a few persons who were prepared to hand over the town. ## modern-en · myrcinians · 15:4

Cleon, whom we left on his voyage from Torone to Amphipolis, made Eion his base. After an unsuccessful assault on the Andrian colony of Stagirus, he took Galepsus, a colony of Thasos, by storm. He now sent envoys to Perdiccas to require his attendance with an army, as the alliance provided, and others to Thrace, to Polles, king of the Odomantians, who was to bring as many Thracian mercenaries as possible. He himself remained inactive at Eion, awaiting their arrival. Informed of this, Brasidas in turn took up a position of observation on Cerdylium, a place on high ground in Argilian territory across the river, not far from Amphipolis. It commanded a view in every direction, so that Cleon's army could not move without his seeing it; for he fully expected that Cleon, despising the small numbers of his opponent, would march against Amphipolis with the force he already had with him. At the same time Brasidas made his preparations, calling to his standard fifteen hundred Thracian mercenaries and all the Edonians, both horse and targeteers. He also had a thousand Myrcinian and Chalcidian targeteers, in addition to those in Amphipolis, and a force of heavy infantry numbering altogether about two thousand, plus three hundred Hellenic horse. Of these, fifteen hundred he had with him on Cerdylium; the rest were stationed with Clearidas in Amphipolis.

Of the Edonian town that came over to Brasidas. One of their targeteers overtook and killed Cleon; their horse and the Chalcidians’ finished the Athenian right.

## modern-en · alcibiades · 16:19

With the breach between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians having gone this far, the party at Athens that wished to cancel the treaty also at once put themselves in motion. Foremost among these was Alcibiades, son of Clinias, a man still young in years for any other Hellenic city but distinguished by the splendor of his ancestry. Alcibiades thought the Argive alliance really preferable, though personal pique also had a great deal to do with his opposition. He was offended with the Lacedaemonians for having negotiated the treaty through Nicias and Laches and overlooked him on account of his youth, and also for not having shown him the respect due to his family's ancient connection with them as their proxeni — a connection his grandfather had renounced, and which he had himself lately thought to renew by his attentions to their prisoners taken on the island. Considering himself slighted on all sides, he had at first spoken against the treaty, saying the Lacedaemonians were not to be trusted, but that they were only treating in order to be enabled by this means to crush Argos, and afterwards to attack Athens alone. Now, immediately after the events above, he sent privately to the Argives, telling them to come as quickly as possible to Athens, accompanied by the Mantineans and Eleans, with proposals of alliance, since the moment was favorable and he himself would do all he could to help them.

Clinias’s son, still young for high office in any other Hellenic city but distinguished by the splendour of his ancestry — and offended that Lacedaemon had made the peace through Nicias and Laches and passed him over. He sent privately to Argos to bring the Argives, Mantineans and Eleans to Athens; trapped the Lacedaemonian envoys into denying in the assembly the full powers they had claimed in the senate, by promising privately to give Pylos back for them; and carried the hundred years’ alliance. Afterwards he marched about the Peloponnese settling the league’s affairs, had the Athenians write on the Laconian pillar that Lacedaemon had not kept her oaths, and when Argos went over at last carried off three hundred suspected men and lodged them in the islands.

## modern-en · cleobulus · 16:11

Next winter, however, the ephors under whom the treaty had been made were no longer in office, and some of their successors were directly opposed to it. Embassies now arrived from the Lacedaemonian confederacy, and the Athenians, Boeotians, and Corinthians also presented themselves at Lacedaemon. After much discussion and no agreement, they separated for their several homes. Cleobulus and Xenares, the two ephors most anxious to break off the treaty, took advantage of this to confer privately with the Boeotians and Corinthians. They advised them to act together as much as possible, and instructed the Boeotians first to enter into alliance with Argos, and then try to bring themselves and the Argives into alliance with Lacedaemon. The Boeotians would in this way be least likely to be forced into the Attic treaty, while the Lacedaemonians would prefer to gain the friendship and alliance of Argos even at the price of war with Athens and the rupture of the treaty. The Boeotians knew that an honorable friendship with Argos had long been desired by Lacedaemon, since the Lacedaemonians believed that this would significantly facilitate the conduct of the war outside the Peloponnese. Meanwhile they begged the Boeotians to put Panactum into Lacedaemonian hands, so that she might if possible obtain Pylos in exchange for it, and so be in a better position to resume hostilities with Athens.

One of the two ephors most anxious to break the treaty off, who took the Boeotians and Corinthians aside and told them to get themselves into alliance with Argos first and with Lacedaemon afterwards.

## modern-en · xenares-cnidis · 16:37

Summer was now over. In the following winter a battle took place between the Heracleots in Trachinia and the Aenianians, Dolopians, Malians, and certain of the Thessalians — all tribes bordering on the town and hostile to it, since it directly threatened their country. Accordingly, having opposed and harassed it from its very foundation by every means in their power, they now in this battle defeated the Heracleots. Xenares, son of Cnidis, their Lacedaemonian commander, was among the slain. Thus the winter ended, and the twelfth year of this war also ended. After the battle, Heraclea was so terribly reduced that in the first days of the following summer the Boeotians occupied the place and sent away the Lacedaemonian Agesippidas for misgovernment, fearing that the town might be taken by the Athenians while the Lacedaemonians were distracted by the affairs of the Peloponnese. The Lacedaemonians, however, were offended with them for what they had done.

Cnidis’s son, the Lacedaemonian commanding at Heraclea in Trachis, and among the slain when the neighbouring tribes beat the Heracleots. The history does not say whether he is the ephor.

## modern-en · eustrophus · 16:16

In the first days of the following summer, the Argives — seeing that the promised ambassadors from Boeotia did not arrive, that Panactum was being demolished, and that a separate alliance had been concluded between the Boeotians and Lacedaemonians — began to fear that Argos might be left isolated and the whole confederacy go over to Lacedaemon. They imagined that the Boeotians had been persuaded by the Lacedaemonians to raze Panactum and to enter into the treaty with the Athenians, and that Athens was privy to this arrangement, so that not even her alliance was open to them any longer — a resource they had always been counting on, given the existing dissensions, in case their treaty with Lacedaemon should not continue. In this strait the Argives, afraid that as a result of refusing to renew the treaty with Lacedaemon and aspiring to the supremacy of the Peloponnese, they would have the Lacedaemonians, Tegeans, Boeotians, and Athenians on their hands all at once, now hastily sent off Eustrophus and Aeson — who seemed the men most likely to be acceptable — as envoys to Lacedaemon, with the aim of making the best treaty they could with the Lacedaemonians on whatever terms they could get, and being left in peace.

One of the two Argives sent to Lacedaemon as the men most likely to be acceptable, to get the best treaty they could and be left in peace. They came back with a fifty years’ truce that left the Cynurian land to be settled, if either side chose, by a formal challenge and a battle.

## modern-en · andromedes · 16:18

The envoys returned accordingly. Meanwhile, while the Argives were engaged in these negotiations, the Lacedaemonian ambassadors — Andromedes, Phaedimus, and Antimenidas — who were to receive the prisoners from the Boeotians and restore them and Panactum to the Athenians, found that the Boeotians had themselves razed Panactum, on the plea that oaths had been anciently exchanged between their people and the Athenians, after a dispute on the subject, to the effect that neither should inhabit the place but they should graze it in common. As for the Athenian prisoners of war held by the Boeotians, these were handed over to Andromedes and his colleagues, who conveyed them to Athens and gave them back. The envoys at the same time announced the razing of Panactum, which to them seemed as good as its restitution, since it would no longer house an enemy of Athens. This announcement was received with great indignation by the Athenians, who thought the Lacedaemonians had played them false — both in the matter of the demolition of Panactum, which ought to have been restored to them standing, and in having, as they now learned, made a separate alliance with the Boeotians, in spite of their previous promise to join Athens in compelling the adhesion of those who refused to accede to the treaty. The Athenians also considered the other points on which Lacedaemon had failed in her compact, and thinking they had been duped, gave an angry answer to the ambassadors and sent them away.

One of the three Lacedaemonians sent to take Panactum and the Athenian prisoners from the Boeotians and hand them back. They found Panactum razed, brought the prisoners to Athens, and announced the demolition as though it were as good as restitution.

## modern-en · androsthenes · 16:35

At the Olympic games held this summer, in which the Arcadian Androsthenes was victor for the first time in the wrestling and boxing, the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple by the Eleans, and thus prevented from sacrificing or competing, because they had refused to pay the fine specified in the Olympic law that the Eleans had imposed on them. The Eleans alleged that they had attacked Fort Phyrcus and had sent heavy infantry of theirs into Lepreum during the Olympic truce. The amount of the fine was two thousand minae — two for each heavy-armed soldier, as the law prescribes. The Lacedaemonians sent envoys and argued that the fine was unjust, claiming that the truce had not yet been proclaimed at Lacedaemon when the heavy infantry were sent off. But the Eleans maintained that the armistice with them had already begun (they proclaim it first among themselves) and that the Lacedaemonian aggression had taken them by surprise while they were living quietly as in peacetime, expecting nothing of the kind. The Lacedaemonians replied that, if the Eleans really believed they had committed aggression, it would have been pointless to proclaim the truce at Lacedaemon afterwards. But they had proclaimed it nonetheless, since they believed nothing of the kind, and from that moment the Lacedaemonians had made no attack on their country. The Eleans, however, stuck to what they had said, that nothing would persuade them that an aggression had not been committed. They added, however, that if the Lacedaemonians would restore Lepreum, they would give up their own share of the money and pay the god's share for them.

An Arcadian, victor for the first time in the wrestling and boxing at the Olympic games from which Lacedaemon was excluded.

Summer was now over. In the following winter a battle took place between the Heracleots in Trachinia and the Aenianians, Dolopians, Malians, and certain of the Thessalians — all tribes bordering on the town and hostile to it, since it directly threatened their country. Accordingly, having opposed and harassed it from its very foundation by every means in their power, they now in this battle defeated the Heracleots. Xenares, son of Cnidis, their Lacedaemonian commander, was among the slain. Thus the winter ended, and the twelfth year of this war also ended. After the battle, Heraclea was so terribly reduced that in the first days of the following summer the Boeotians occupied the place and sent away the Lacedaemonian Agesippidas for misgovernment, fearing that the town might be taken by the Athenians while the Lacedaemonians were distracted by the affairs of the Peloponnese. The Lacedaemonians, however, were offended with them for what they had done.

## modern-en · hipponoidas · 16:56

Just before the battle was joined, King Agis decided on the following maneuver. All armies are alike in this: as they go into action they get pushed out rather to the right, and each side overlaps with this its adversary's left. Fear makes every man do his best to shelter his unarmed side with the shield of the man next to him on the right, thinking the closer the shields are locked together, the better protected he will be. The man primarily responsible for this is the one on the extreme right, who is always trying to withdraw his unarmed side from the enemy, and the same fear makes the rest follow him. On the present occasion the Mantineans extended with their wing far beyond the Sciritae, and the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans even farther beyond the Athenians, since their army was the largest. Agis, afraid of his left being surrounded, and thinking the Mantineans outflanked it too far, ordered the Sciritae and Brasideans to move out from their place in the ranks and make the line even with the Mantineans. He told the Polemarchs Hipponoidas and Aristocles to fill the gap thus formed by throwing themselves into it with two companies taken from the right wing, thinking his right would still be strong enough and to spare, and that the line facing the Mantineans would gain in solidity.

One of the two polemarchs ordered, in the moment of the onset at Mantinea, to fill the gap Agis had just opened on his own left. He would not move over, and was banished from Sparta afterwards on the charge of cowardice.

## modern-en · endius · 16:21

At the same time an embassy arrived in haste from Lacedaemon, made up of men reputed to be well disposed toward the Athenians — Philocharidas, Leon, and Endius. They were sent for fear that the Athenians in their irritation might conclude an alliance with the Argives, and also to ask back Pylos in exchange for Panactum, and to plead in defence of the alliance with the Boeotians that it had not been made to harm the Athenians. When the envoys spoke in the senate on these points and stated that they had come with full powers to settle all matters at issue between the two states, Alcibiades became afraid that, if they repeated these statements to the popular assembly, they might win over the multitude and the Argive alliance might be rejected. So he had recourse to the following stratagem. He persuaded the Lacedaemonians by a solemn assurance that, if they would say nothing about their full powers in the assembly, he would give Pylos back to them — he himself, the present opponent of its restitution, undertaking to obtain this from the Athenians — and would settle the other points at issue. His plan was to detach them from Nicias and to disgrace them before the people as having no sincerity in their intentions, or even common consistency in their language, and so to get the Argives, Eleans, and Mantineans taken into alliance. The plan succeeded. When the envoys appeared before the people, and on the question being put to them did not say, as they had said in the senate, that they had come with full powers, the Athenians lost all patience. Carried away by Alcibiades, who thundered more loudly than ever against the Lacedaemonians, they were ready to introduce the Argives and their companions on the spot and take them into alliance. An earthquake occurred, however, before anything definite had been done, and this assembly was adjourned.

One of the three Lacedaemonians reputed well disposed toward Athens, sent in haste to keep the Argive alliance from being made — and made to look insincere in the assembly by Alcibiades.

At this point word arrived from their friends in Tegea that, unless they came quickly, Tegea would go over from them to the Argives and their allies, if it had not gone over already. On this news a force marched out from Lacedaemon — Spartans and Helots and all their people — at once, and on a scale never before seen. Advancing as far as Orestheum in Maenalia, they ordered the Arcadians of their league to follow close after them to Tegea. ## modern-en · lepreans · 16:6

Immediately afterwards an Elean embassy arrived. Having first made an alliance with Corinth, they went on from there to Argos, according to their instructions, and became allies of the Argives, their country being just then at enmity with Lacedaemon and Lepreum. Some time before, there had been a war between the Lepreans and some of the Arcadians. The Eleans, called in by the Lepreans with the offer of half their lands, had ended the war, leaving the land in the hands of its Leprean occupiers but imposing on them the tribute of a talent to Olympian Zeus. Until the Attic war this tribute was paid by the Lepreans, who then took the war as an excuse to stop paying. When the Eleans used force, the Lepreans appealed to Lacedaemon. The case was thus submitted to her arbitration, but the Eleans, suspecting the fairness of the tribunal, withdrew the reference and laid waste the Leprean territory. The Lacedaemonians nevertheless decided that the Lepreans were independent and the Eleans the aggressors, and as the Eleans did not abide by the arbitration, they sent a garrison of heavy infantry into Lepreum. At this the Eleans, holding that Lacedaemon had received one of their rebel subjects, invoked the convention providing that each confederate should come out of the Attic war in possession of what he had when he went into it. Considering that justice had not been done them, they went over to the Argives, and now made the alliance through their ambassadors, who had been instructed for the purpose. Immediately after them the Corinthians and the Thracian Chalcidians became allies of Argos. Meanwhile the Boeotians and Megarians, who acted together, kept quiet, being left to do as they pleased by Lacedaemon, and thinking that the Argive democracy would not suit their aristocratic government as well as the Lacedaemonian constitution.

Who gave the Eleans half their land for ending a war with the Arcadians, paid the talent to Olympian Zeus until the Attic war gave them an excuse to stop, and appealed to Lacedaemon when Elis used force. Lacedaemon declared them independent and put a garrison in, and Elis went over to Argos.

## modern-en · dians · 16:10

The same summer the Dians took Thyssus, a town on Acte by Athos in alliance with Athens. Throughout the whole of this summer relations between the Athenians and Peloponnesians continued, although each side began to suspect the other immediately after the treaty, because the places named in it had not been restored. Lacedaemon, whose lot it was to begin by giving back Amphipolis and the other towns, had not done so. She had equally failed to get the treaty accepted by her Thracian allies, or by the Boeotians or Corinthians, although she was continually promising to join with Athens in compelling their compliance if it were any longer refused. She kept fixing dates after which those who still refused to come in were to be declared enemies to both sides, but took care not to bind herself by any written agreement. Meanwhile the Athenians, seeing none of these professions actually carried out, began to suspect the honesty of her intentions. Consequently they not only refused to comply with her demands for Pylos but also regretted having given up the prisoners from the island, and held tight to the other places until Lacedaemon had fulfilled her part of the treaty. Lacedaemon, on her part, said she had done what she could: she had given up the Athenian prisoners of war in her possession, evacuated Thrace, and performed everything else within her power. Restoring Amphipolis was beyond her ability, but she would try to bring the Boeotians and Corinthians into the treaty, to recover Panactum, and to send home all the Athenian prisoners of war in Boeotia. Meanwhile she required that Pylos be restored, or at any rate that the Messenians and Helots be withdrawn — as her own troops had been from Thrace — and the place garrisoned, if necessary, by the Athenians themselves. After a number of conferences during the summer, she succeeded in persuading Athens to withdraw from Pylos the Messenians and the rest of the Helots and deserters from Laconia, who were accordingly settled by her at Cranii in Cephallenia. Thus during this summer there was peace and intercourse between the two peoples.

Of Dium on Athos, who took Thyssus from the Athenian alliance, and who revolted to the Chalcidians themselves two years later.

## modern-en · patrians · 16:38

The same summer Alcibiades, son of Clinias, now one of the generals at Athens, acting in concert with the Argives and the allies, went into the Peloponnese with a few Athenian heavy infantry and archers and some of the allies in those parts whom he took up as he passed. With this army he marched here and there through the Peloponnese, settling various matters connected with the alliance. Among other things, he induced the Patrians to carry their walls down to the sea, intending himself also to build a fort near the Achaean Rhium. However, the Corinthians and Sicyonians, and all others who would have suffered by its being built, came up and stopped him.

Whom Alcibiades induced to carry their walls down to the sea.

## modern-en · orchomenians-arcadia · 16:47

After this a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and three hundred horse arrived, under the command of Laches and Nicostratus. The Argives, still unwilling to break the truce with the Lacedaemonians, begged them to depart and refused to bring them before the people, to whom they had a communication to make, until they were forced to do so by the entreaties of the Mantineans and Eleans, who were still at Argos. The Athenians, through the mouth of Alcibiades, their ambassador on the spot, told the Argives and the allies that they had no right to make a truce at all without the consent of their fellow confederates, and that now that the Athenians had so opportunely arrived, the war ought to be resumed. These arguments succeeded with the allies, and they immediately marched on Orchomenos, all except the Argives, who, although they had consented like the rest, stayed behind at first but eventually joined the others. They all now sat down and besieged Orchomenos and made assaults on it. One of their reasons for wanting to take this place was that hostages from Arcadia had been lodged there by the Lacedaemonians. The Orchomenians, alarmed by the weakness of their wall and the size of the enemy force, and by the danger of being destroyed before relief arrived, surrendered on condition of joining the league, of giving hostages of their own to the Mantineans, and of giving up those lodged with them by the Lacedaemonians. With Orchomenos thus secured, the allies now consulted on which of the remaining places they should attack next. The Eleans pressed for Lepreum, the Mantineans for Tegea. The Argives and Athenians supported the Mantineans, and the Eleans, furious at not getting their vote for Lepreum, went home. The rest of the allies prepared at Mantinea to march against Tegea, where a faction inside had arranged to put the place into their hands.

Of Orchomenos in Arcadia, where Lacedaemon had lodged her Arcadian hostages. Alarmed by a weak wall and a large army, they joined the league, gave hostages of their own to Mantinea, and gave up the ones they were holding. Not the Boeotians of the same name.

## modern-en · cleomedes · 17:0

The next summer Alcibiades sailed with twenty ships to Argos and seized the suspected men still left of the Lacedaemonian faction, to the number of three hundred. ## modern-en · philocrates · 17:33

Summer was now over. The following winter the Lacedaemonians intended to invade Argive territory, but on reaching the frontier they found the sacrifices for crossing unfavorable and went back again. This intention of theirs gave the Argives suspicions of certain of their fellow citizens, some of whom they arrested, though others escaped them. About the same time the Melians again took another part of the Athenian lines, which were only feebly garrisoned. When reinforcements arrived from Athens in consequence, under the command of Philocrates son of Demeas, the siege was now pressed vigorously. With some treachery occurring inside, the Melians surrendered at discretion to the Athenians, who put to death all the grown men they took, and sold the women and children as slaves. They afterwards sent out five hundred colonists and settled the place themselves.

Demeas’s son, who brought the reinforcements that pressed the siege of Melos to its end.
